Crossing beyond scattering amplitudes
Simon Caron-Huot, Mathieu Giroux, Holmfridur S. Hannesdottir, Sebastian Mizera

Abstract
We find that different asymptotic measurements in quantum field theory can be related to one another through new versions of crossing symmetry . Assuming analyticity, we conjecture generalized crossing relations for multi-particle processes and the corresponding paths of analytic continuation. We prove them to all multiplicity at tree-level in quantum field theory and string theory. We illustrate how to practically perform analytic continuations on loop-level examples using different methods, including unitarity cuts and differential equations. We study the extent to which anomalous thresholds away from the usual physical region can cause an analytic obstruction to crossing when massless particles are involved. In an appendix, we review and streamline historical proofs of four-particle crossing symmetry in gapped theories.



1
Introduction

Crossing symmetry states that particles can be interpreted as anti-particles traveling backward in time. More precisely, it means that scattering amplitudes in different kinematic channels are analytic continuations of one and the same function. This proposal equips us with a powerful computational tool: if one, for example, knows the scattering amplitude for electron-positron annihilation,
e^{-}e^{+}\to\gamma\gamma
, then the amplitude for Compton scattering
e^{-}\gamma\to e^{-}\gamma
can simply be obtained by analytic continuation, as illustrated below in Fig.
1
.
Since its proposal in 1954
Gell-Mann:1954ttj
, crossing symmetry has grown to be widely accepted as a fact of life with many applications, including to dispersion relations, though its theoretical foundations have remained arguably on shaky grounds beyond the simplest cases.
For example, even though Feynman diagrams for crossed processes
look
the same, since they are obviously built out of the same propagators and vertices with simply some energy signs changed, this by no means guarantees that the resulting functions are
continuously
related by a path of analytic continuation.

In the case of
2\to 2
scattering of stable particles in mass-gapped theories, crossing symmetry was rigorously proven by Bros, Epstein, and Glaser in the 1960s
Bros:1964iho
;
Bros:1965kbd
within the framework of axiomatic field theory. The proof involves two main parts: first, showing that there exists a region in the
off-shell
kinematic space for which Green’s functions corresponding to two physical channels are the same, and second—vastly more difficult—that there exists an analytic continuation between these Green’s functions purely within the
on-shell
kinematics. Since then, there has been intermittent progress on crossing symmetry, including an extension of the proof to the
2\to 3
case in
Bros:1972jh
;
Bros:1985gy
, and more recently a perturbative proof of crossing in the planar limit for any multiplicities and masses in
Mizera:2021fap
.

In this paper, we take a step towards understanding crossing for scattering at higher points by asking: assuming that an analytic path interchanging some incoming particles to outgoing anti-particles exists, what is the result of the continuation? For instance, what could we reasonably expect to be the result of crossing the photon and the positron in the
e^{-}\gamma\to e^{-}e^{-}e^{+}
process? Naively, based on the physical arguments of a symmetry between particles and anti-particles, one could expect that the answer is the amplitude in the crossed channel, or perhaps its complex conjugate.

Figure 1
:
Crossing symmetry illustrated on a
2\to 2
scattering processes. If we cross an electron and photon in Compton scattering,
e^{-}\gamma\to e^{-}\gamma
on the right, we end up with electron-photon annihilation,
e^{+}e^{-}\to\gamma\gamma
on the left. The particles that cross are colored in red. The Mandelstam invariant
s
crosses from being positive in one process to negative in the other. Note that time flows from right to left in these diagrams.

Remarkably, it turns out that crossing is much richer: it does not only relate scattering amplitudes to each other, but rather, it relates different types of observables! A simple way to motivate this idea is to recall why amplitudes are analytic in the first place. The traditional explanation involves microcausality: vanishing of spacelike commutators makes momentum-space correlators analytic in some domains, as reviewed below.
The appearance of commutators suggests that analytic continuation can modify the operator ordering, and thus lead to observables in which the time ordering of operators is relaxed.

There are many contexts in which such observables occur
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
. For example, when the scattered objects have a large degeneracy of internal states, exclusive S-matrix elements between individual initial and final states are typically entropically suppressed
\sim\mathrm{e}^{-S/2}
and can exhibit a high sensitivity to the details of initial and final states.
In such situations, “in-in” expectation values, where one inclusively sums over unobserved final states, are typically closer to experiment and simultaneously easier to calculate using either many-body tools or semi-classical approximations. As another example, according to the Kosower–Maybee–O’Connell (KMOC) formalism
Kosower:2018adc
;
Cristofoli:2021vyo
, on-shell in-in observables can describe gravitational waveforms as detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA detectors
LIGOScientific:2016aoc
;
LIGOScientific:2017vwq
;
LIGOScientific:2017ync
, whether or not the participating black holes or compact objects have a large entropy. The waveform in a related scattering problem is then computed as the expectation value of a graviton in the background of black-hole scattering (which can be related to the emission from bound orbits using effective field theory logic).
The KMOC formalism has recently been used to compute gravitational waveforms in perturbation theory by modeling the black holes as heavy scalars
Brandhuber:2023hhy
;
Herderschee:2023fxh
;
Elkhidir:2023dco
;
Georgoudis:2023lgf
;
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
.

The general non-time-ordered observables that will appear in this paper can be characterized by arbitrary strings of creation/annihilation operators,
a^{\dagger}
/
a
and

b^{\dagger}
/
b
, that, respectively, act in the far past and future.
Besides in-in expectation values and inclusive cross sections, these include more exotic out-of-time-order amplitudes that have been classified in a recent paper
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, which also gave various methods to compute them. Thus, we will find that
analyticity of the S-matrix unites families of asymptotic observables. This statement is powerful, since knowing one asymptotic observable in a family, others can be computed simply by analytic continuation.
It also means that aspects of one observable, such as symbol properties, automatically translate to the others.

The crossing paths we will consider involve a set of particles that are highly boosted along a specific lightcone direction, say the “
p^{+}
” direction. We will use a single complex variable
z
to apply a complex boost to these particles while staying entirely on-shell, thus rotating some momenta from incoming to outgoing and vice versa. This complex boost coincides with a standard CPT transformation
Streater:1989vi
, however one which acts on only a
subset
of the momenta.
We stress that, because this complex boost is not applied to all momenta, crossing symmetry does not merely follow from CPT invariance of amplitudes.

The result of applying this continuation to the
2\to 3
process
e^{-}\gamma\to e^{-}e^{-}e^{+}
is shown in Fig.
2
: for
z<0
it yields an inclusive measurement of the photon field in the background of an
e^{-}e^{-}
. Replacing the electrons with black holes (or other compact objects), and the photon by a graviton, yields the gravitational waveform mentioned above. This is a striking result: inclusive waveforms can be computed by analytically continuing the
exclusive
amplitude for a graviton and black hole to scatter into two black holes and an anti-black hole!

Crossing symmetry illustrated on a

processes. We cross an electron (photon) in the scattering process

from outgoing (incoming), using a path parameterized by

z>0

z<0

X

, our main conjectured

crossing equation
predicts what happens when we cross an incoming single-particle state
B
with an outgoing
C

(1)

Following
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, we use conventions in which operator
products are taken from right to left, as in bra-ket notation (so time flows to the left in the
S
-blobs).
The dashed lines represent cuts that sum over the intermediate on-shell states
X
and
Y
and integrate over their phase space with positive energies.

The above conjecture will be motivated by rigorous manipulations of off-shell correlators. We thus expect it to hold when the corresponding analyticity properties extend to the mass shell, which we will physically argue for in some situations. Rigorously proving that last part, similarly to
Bros:1964iho
;
Bros:1965kbd
;
Bros:1971ghu
;
Bros:1985gy
, will require efforts that are beyond the scope of this paper.
Our main goal is to elucidate what statements of crossing and microcausality can actually be valid beyond
2\to 2
, and to test them in examples. Our results are not restricted to axiomatic field theory, and we consider various processes order-by-order in perturbation theory, as well as individual diagrams with massless and massive internal particles in dimensional regularization.

In Sec.
2
we recall the main axioms of S-matrix theory and how they naturally allow for generalized (non-time-ordered) amplitudes;
we also review the classical arguments linking microcausality and analyticity, highlighting subtleties with the on-shell limits.
In Sec.
3
we combine these ideas to formulate the crossing equation (
1
), illustrating in simple tree-level and one-loop cases why all factors are necessary.
We speculate in Sec.
3.5
on a minimal extension to general multi-particle clusters
A,B,C
and
D
. Intriguingly, this extension makes diagrammatic sense, but cannot be written as a string of operators acting on a Hilbert space.

We will stress that crossing is already non-trivial at
tree level
if one pays close attention to the
i\varepsilon
prescriptions in the propagators of (unstable) heavy intermediate particles. In Sec.
4
we give a combinatorial proof that our conjecture (including its speculative multi-particle extension) holds at tree level for any multiplicity.

In Sec.
5
we continue our investigations to one loop
and consider all master integrals for massless five-particle amplitudes. The crossing equation relates various amplitudes and cuts in different channels, which we test using a variety of techniques for analytic continuation of (i) closed-form expressions, (ii) loop-momentum Feynman integrals, (iii) Schwinger-parametrized integrals, and (iv) differential equations. The crossing equation is verified by comparing these results to direct computations of unitarity cuts.
We also highlight the existence of moves which relate (ordinary) amplitudes to amplitudes, leading to non-trivial relations between integration constants in different channels for the differential equation method.

The prerequisite for crossing to work, i.e., that amplitudes are actually analytic on the mass shell along the considered path, is not merely a mathematical detail waiting to be eventually ironed out.
In Sec.
6
we give a non-trivial counterexample,
involving massive external legs and a massless internal particle,
where our crossing conjecture fails as a result of landing
us on the “wrong side” of an anomalous threshold branch cut. We introduce an extension of the Coleman–Norton picture of anomalous thresholds to illustrate how this phenomenon is caused by internal particles moving faster than the crossed external ones, thus highlighting
the importance of a mass gap in the arguments from the last century.
However, we will also observe that even in gapless theories,
certain crossing moves, including the one in Fig.
2
, appear to be immune from this phenomenon,
suggesting that a mass gap is not always necessary.

In Sec.
7
we analyze the predictions of crossing for tree-level string amplitudes. Analytic continuation can be achieved directly by contour manipulations on the moduli space of Riemann surfaces. After reviewing how to see unitarity cuts from this perspective, we give an example of an in-in observable in string theory by crossing from a time-ordered amplitude and numerically plot the corresponding space-time geometry.
In Sec.
8
we present our conclusions.

In App.
A
we offer simplified physicist-level versions of the axiomatic field theory proofs of crossing symmetry and of analyticity near the mass shell. We highlight powerful simplifications and theorems that have been developed in the 1970’s, a decade after the most-cited results were initially obtained, in the hope that these will help answer the questions raised in this work. The remaining appendices give details of technical computations: embedding-space formulae for cuts in App.
B
, differential equations for massless pentagon diagram in App.
C
, and numerical approach to solving differential equations in App.
D
.

Notations and conventions

We work in
\mathrm{D}
spacetime dimensions, and take momentum components of
p^{\mu}
to be
p^{\mu}=(p^{0},p^{1},\ldots,p^{\mathrm{D}-1})
. The spatial part of
p^{\mu}
is labeled with
\vec{p}=(p^{1},\ldots,p^{\mathrm{D}-1})
. We work in mostly-plus signature where
p^{2}=-(p^{0})^{2}+(p^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(p^{\mathrm{D}-1})^{2}
and all-outgoing conventions in which
p_{i}^{0}<0
for incoming particles and
p_{i}^{0}>0
for the outgoing ones. When using lightcone coordinates, we define

p^{\pm}=p^{0}\pm p^{\mathrm{D}-1}\,,\quad p^{\perp}=(p^{1},\ldots,p^{\mathrm{D}-2})\,,

(2)

and hence
p^{2}=-p^{+}p^{-}+(p^{\perp})^{2}
.
To summarize, we will use the following terminology:

Future timelike:

\displaystyle p^{0}>0\,,

\displaystyle\quad p^{2}<0\,,

(3)

Past timelike:

\displaystyle p^{0}<0\,,

\displaystyle\quad p^{2}<0\,,

(4)

Spacelike:

\displaystyle\bullet

\displaystyle\quad p^{2}>0\,.

(5)

We use the notation
p_{ij\cdots k}^{\mu}=p_{i}^{\mu}+p_{j}^{\mu}+\ldots+p_{k}^{\mu}
, and
s_{ij\cdots k}=-p_{ij\cdots k}^{2}
for Mandelstam invariants.

The connected interacting part
T
of the S-matrix is obtained as usual with

S=\mathbbm{1}+iT+\ldots\,,

(6)

where the dots include disconnected products of
T
’s (that are only present at high multiplicity).
The interacting part of the scattering amplitude,
\mathcal{M}
, is obtained as the matrix element of
T
with the overall momentum-conserving delta function factored out:
\mathcal{M}_{f\leftarrow i}=\langle f|T|i\rangle(2\pi)^{\mathrm{D}}\delta^{\mathrm{D}}(\sum_{i}p_{i}^{\mu})
.

We draw diagrams to follow the ordering of operators in bra-ket notation, so that time flows towards the
left
in scattering amplitudes
S
or
\mathcal{M}
, and towards the right in conjugated amplitudes
S^{\dagger}
or
\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}
factors.

2
Background

In this section, we review some background material on the S-matrix, ranging from the algebra of asymptotic creation/annihilation operators to causality and crossing symmetry.

2.1
Review of S-matrix axioms

In this paper, we use manipulations in axiomatic field theory to motivate our formulae and conjectures for scattering amplitudes and other asymptotic observables. In a recent paper
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, we detailed the necessary axioms of S-matrix theory, explained the blob notation and how to efficiently compute asymptotic observables. Here, we provide a brief review of these points.

We assume the existence of an
asymptotic algebra
separately in the far past and far future. In the far past, we have asymptotic creation (annihilation) operators,
a_{i}^{\dagger}
(
a_{i}
), for each particle
i
, which satisfy the usual commutation relations

[a_{i},a^{\dagger}_{j}]=\delta_{i,j}\ 2|p_{i}^{0}|\ (2\pi)^{\mathrm{D}-1}\delta^{\mathrm{D}-1}(\vec{p}_{i}-\vec{p}_{j})\,.

(7)

The Kronecker delta function
\delta_{i,j}
ensures that the flavor and spin indices, which are included in the labels
i
and
j
, are the same and
p_{i}^{0}
is the energy of particle
i
. We assume an analogous algebra in the far future, where the operators are labeled as
b_{i}
and
b_{i}^{\dagger}
.
2
2

2

Note that the literature often uses
a_{i}^{\text{in}}
and
a_{i}^{\text{out}}
for the operators
a_{i}
and
b_{i}
, respectively. Here we use
a
’s and
b
’s instead for clarity.
These operators act on equivalent Hilbert spaces. In particular, we assume the existence of a time-invariant vacuum,
|0\rangle
, which is annihilated by all the
a_{i}
and all the
b_{i}
. The operators in the past and future are related by a unitary evolution operator,
S
, according to

b_{i}=S^{\dagger}a_{i}S\,,

(8)

and its conjugate
b_{i}^{\dagger}=S^{\dagger}a_{i}^{\dagger}S
. The evolution operator acts trivially on the vacuum,

S|0\rangle=S^{\dagger}|0\rangle=|0\rangle.

(9)

We also assume that one-particle states are stable, which means that

Sa_{i}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=S^{\dagger}a_{i}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=a_{i}^{\dagger}|0\rangle,

(10)

along with the analogous equations obtained by replacing
a_{i}^{\dagger}
with
b_{i}^{\dagger}
. We frequently use the shorthand notation
|i\cdots j\rangle\equiv a_{i}^{\dagger}\cdots a_{j}^{\dagger}|0\rangle
and
\langle i\cdots j|\equiv\langle 0|a_{i}\cdots a_{j}
. Notice, in particular, that states such as
|i\cdots j\rangle
are taken by default to live in the far past.

This setup can be applied to any quantum field theory in which the conventional S-matrix makes sense, such as pion scattering in four dimensions or perturbative QCD in dimensional regularization.

Equipped with these rules, we can build various objects that we call
asymptotic observables
by stringing together creation and annihilation operators. For example, we can string together three
b_{i}
’s and two
a_{i}^{\dagger}
’s to get

\langle 0|b_{5}b_{4}b_{3}a_{2}^{\dagger}a_{1}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=\langle 0|S^{\dagger}a_{5}SS^{\dagger}a_{4}SS^{\dagger}a_{3}Sa_{2}^{\dagger}a_{1}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=\langle 0|a_{5}a_{4}a_{3}Sa_{2}^{\dagger}a_{1}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=\langle 345|S|12\rangle\,,

(11)

which is the usual (time-ordered) scattering amplitude for
12\to 345
. To match with the time-ordering in these expressions, we will henceforth write such an amplitude using the mirrored convention
345\leftarrow 12
. An analogous derivation shows that the
m\leftarrow n
scattering amplitude
\langle n+1\cdots n+m|S|12\cdots n\rangle
is obtained by stringing
m
operators of
b_{i}
type with
n
operators of
a_{i}^{\dagger}
type.

Scattering amplitudes comprise only a small number of possible strings of creation and annihilation operators. We can, for example, form the following observable,

\mathrm{Exp}_{3}\equiv\langle 0|a_{5}a_{4}b_{3}a_{2}^{\dagger}a_{1}^{\dagger}|0\rangle=\langle 45|S^{\dagger}a_{3}S|12\rangle=\sumint_{X}\langle 45|S^{\dagger}|X\rangle\langle X3|S|12\rangle\,,

(12)

where we have inserted a complete set of states
\mathbbm{1}=\sumint_{X}|X\rangle\langle X|
in the rightmost equality. This represents the inclusive amplitude for measuring the particle labeled by
3
in the background of
45\leftarrow 12
scattering, and it is important enough so that we give it a name:
\mathrm{Exp}_{3}
. As discussed in detail in
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, this type of measurement is relevant when the scattered particles have many internal states, in which the exclusive scattering amplitude for producing particle
3
is suppressed. The relevant object is rather an inclusive observable, where the in-states
|12\rangle
and
|45\rangle
are integrated against the same wavefunction, and we measure
3
after the collision, while being inclusive over anything that might have happened after the scattering. It has been used, for example, in the KMOC formalism
Kosower:2018adc
to compute the gravitational waveform emitted by scattering of two black holes.

At higher points we can form even more asymptotic observables. For example, at six points, we can build an out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC),
\langle 0|a_{6}b_{5}a_{4}b^{\dagger}_{3}a^{\dagger}_{2}a^{\dagger}_{1}|0\rangle
, or inclusive cross sections, such as
\lim_{4\to 3}\langle 0|a_{6}a_{5}b^{\dagger}_{4}b_{3}a^{\dagger}_{2}a^{\dagger}_{1}|0\rangle=\sumint_{X}\langle 56|S^{\dagger}|3X\rangle\langle X3|S|12\rangle
. As the number of external particles
n
grows larger, scattering amplitudes account for ever-smaller fraction of the total possibilities for forming asymptotic observables to ultimately become of measure zero.

We represent asymptotic observables diagrammatically by rewriting all operators in the future using the relation
b_{i}=S^{\dagger}a_{i}S
, and inserting a complete set of states. As an example, for the OTOC above, we write

\langle 0|b_{6}b_{5}a_{4}b^{\dagger}_{3}a^{\dagger}_{2}a^{\dagger}_{1}|0\rangle=\sumint_{X,Y}\langle 56|S|X\rangle\langle X4|S^{\dagger}|Y3\rangle\langle Y|S|12\rangle\,,

(13)

which we then represent diagrammatically as

time
time
time
5
6
1
2
3
4
S
S^{\dagger}
S
\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}}
\mathord{\raise 0.49991pt\hbox{$\displaystyle Y$}}

(14)

The diagram portrays how we broke the OTOC into the following contributions: the scattering amplitude for
Y\leftarrow 12
, the conjugated amplitude for
X4\leftarrow Y3
, and the amplitude for
56\leftarrow X
. Here, both
X
and
Y
are inclusively summed and integrated over, that is, we add a phase-space integral of the form
\sumint_{X}=\sum_{X_{j}\in X}\prod_{i\in X_{j}}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}q_{i}}{(2\pi)^{\mathrm{D}-1}}\delta^{+}(q_{i}^{2}+m_{i}^{2})
for any set of states
X_{j}
that can take part in the process.
Note that to mirror the convention for the ordering of asymptotic creation/annihilation operators, our convention is that time flows from right to left in the blob diagrams.

2.2
Causality and crossing: Naive, but not too naive

Crossing symmetry of
2\leftarrow 2
scattering amplitudes is well-established in the context of axiomatic quantum field theory for theories with a mass gap, i.e., where all particles in the spectrum have positive masses
Bros:1965kbd
. In this subsection, we briefly review the argument in a way that will highlight the new complications at higher multiplicities (
n>4
particles). To avoid clutter, we discuss below a real scalar theory with a single field
\phi
, normalized such that its two-point function features a canonically normalized pole. We comment on spin later in the next section.

The conventional axiomatic approach involves considering
retarded commutators
of currents in scattering states
Bros:1965kbd
;
Sommer:1970mr
;
Bogolyubov:1990kw
,

\mathcal{R}(p_{3},p_{2})=\int\text{d}^{\mathrm{D}}x_{3}~\text{d}^{\mathrm{D}}x_{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-ip_{2}{\cdot}x_{2}-ip_{3}{\cdot}x_{3}}\,\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,[j(x_{3}),j(x_{2})]_{R}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle\,.

(15)

Here, the
current

j(x)=i(-\partial_{x}^{2}+m^{2})\phi(x)

is the derivative of a local field
\phi(x)
and the
retarded product
of fields is defined as
3
3

3

The
R
-product (
16
) is to be understood as an operation on fields, similar to the time-ordering symbol, such that derivatives in the current
are allowed to act on the
\theta
-function:
[\partial^{\mu}\phi(x),\phi(y)]_{R}\equiv\partial_{x}^{\mu}\left([\phi(x),\phi(y)]_{R}\right)
.
In this setup, (
15
) is analogous to the standard time-ordered LSZ formula, where derivatives acting on
\theta
are also necessary to correctly account for vertices where two or more external legs join.

[\phi(x),\phi(y)]_{R}=[\phi(x),\phi(y)]\theta(x^{0}-y^{0})\,.

(16)

Note that the effect of each
(-\partial_{x}^{2}+m^{2})
in the correlation function is simply to amputate external-leg poles at
p^{2}+m^{2}=0
(after Fourier transform) as in the standard LSZ reduction formula. The retarded product is sandwiched between two strings of asymptotic creation and annihilation operators
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{D}
, for example
\mathcal{A}=a_{1}^{\dagger}
and
\mathcal{D}=b_{4}
.

As we will see, for real positive energy
p_{3}^{0}
, (
15
) evaluates to the amplitude for a certain process, and for real negative
p_{3}^{0}
, it evaluates to that of another process when the momenta are taken to be on shell.
The key idea is then to use analyticity to relate these two processes.
It turns out that analyticity will come about because the retarded product (
16
) vanishes unless
x^{\mu}
lies inside the
future
lightcone
V^{+}
of
y^{\mu}
thanks to the
\theta
-function. Consequently, its Fourier transform (
15
) is analytic in some domain. It includes, off-shell, the upper-half energy plane. Let us now make all of this precise.

Retarded product for real momenta

The first step is to evaluate (
15
) for real and on-shell momenta. On-shell, the current is a total derivative, namely

j(p)\equiv\int\text{d}^{\mathrm{D}}x\,\mathrm{e}^{-ip{\cdot}x}j(x)\xrightarrow{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{on-shell:}}}{{p^{2}\to-m^{2}}}}\int\text{d}^{\mathrm{D}}x\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\mu}}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-ip{\cdot}x}\ (-i\partial^{\mu}_{x}+p^{\mu})\phi(x)\right]\,.

(17)

Observe that this is solely an identity about the Fourier transform of a distribution, and we have not yet made use of the equations of motion. Instead, the dynamics comes into play through the presumption that the product
\mathrm{e}^{-ip{\cdot}x}\phi(x)
undergoes rapid oscillations as
x
approaches infinity,
except
potentially along the paths
x^{\mu}\propto\pm p^{\mu}
of particles heading towards infinity. As a result, after integrating against a smooth function of the (on-shell) momentum
p
, on-shell currents are reduced to surface terms along the direction of particles, thereby naturally giving rise to asymptotic creation and annihilation operators:

\lim_{p^{2}\to-m^{2}}j(p)\equiv\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}a^{\dagger}_{-p}-b^{\dagger}_{-p}&p^{0}<0\quad(\text{incoming})\,,\\
b_{p}-a_{p}&p^{0}>0\quad(\text{outgoing})\,.\end{array}\right.

(18)

The argument presented above is recognizable from textbook derivations of the LSZ reduction formula (see, for instance,
Srednicki:2007qs
). That said, the
a_{p}
and
b^{\dagger}_{-p}
terms are usually omitted in textbooks, given that they vanish for vacuum time-ordered correlators, wherein fields only carry negative frequency components in the past (and positive frequency in the future). Nevertheless, when different operator orderings are taken into consideration, all terms matter. Many examples of reduction formulae obtained from (
18
) were recently discussed in
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
.

When applying the total-derivative argument (
17
) to the Fourier transform of (
16
) with respect to
x_{2}
, one finds surface terms exclusively at past infinity because of the step function:

\lim_{p_{2}^{2}\to-m^{2}}[j(x_{3}),j(p_{2})]_{R}=\begin{cases}~[j(x_{3}),a^{\dagger}_{2}-b^{\dagger}_{2}]&p_{2}^{0}<0\,,\\
-[j(x_{3}),a_{2}-b_{2}]\qquad&p_{2}^{0}>0\,,\end{cases}

(19)

where we used the shorthand notation
a^{\dagger}_{2}=a^{\dagger}_{-p_{2}}
and
a_{2}=a_{p_{2}}
, and similarly for the
b
’s/
b^{\dagger}
’s.

Below, the regime relevant to crossing is when
p_{3}
and
p_{2}
have the largest energies in the problem. By momentum conservation, their energies necessarily have opposite signs, and we also assume that
p_{2}^{\mu}+p_{3}^{\mu}\neq 0
, i.e., the two particles are not forward with each other.
The Fourier transform with respect to
x_{3}
of the first line of (
19
)
then reduces to
[b_{3}-a_{3},a^{\dagger}_{2}-b^{\dagger}_{2}]=[b_{3},a^{\dagger}_{2}]
.
Furthermore, we can drop one term in the commutator since
b_{3}\mathcal{A}|0\rangle=0
due to energy considerations (if
|p_{3}^{0}|
is larger than the energy of the states in
\mathcal{A}
). Analogous comments apply to the second line in (
19
).
Thus, on shell, we have

\mathcal{R}(p_{3},p_{2})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,b_{3}a^{\dagger}_{2}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle,&p_{3}^{0}\sim{-}p_{2}^{0}>0,\quad p_{3}^{0}\gg\mbox{all other energies}\,,\\
-\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,a_{2}b^{\dagger}_{3}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle,&p_{2}^{0}\sim{-}p_{3}^{0}>0,\quad p_{2}^{0}\gg\mbox{all other energies}\,.\end{array}\right.

(20)

This completes our evaluation of
\mathcal{R}
for real momenta.
Note that when either
\mathcal{A}
or
\mathcal{D}
creates a multi-particle state, the second line of (
20
) is not a conventional scattering amplitude.
Fig.
3
sketches how analytic continuation in energy relates these two objects. The deformation parameter
z
will be defined more carefully later in Sec.
3.1
.

z
\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,b_{3}a_{2}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle
-\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,a_{2}b_{3}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle
\mathcal{R}(p_{3},p_{2})

Figure 3
:
The retarded product provides a path of analytic continuation between the two observables shown on the right and on the left.

Analyticity of the retarded product

Analyticity of
\mathcal{R}
at complex momenta
finds its root in the support of (
16
), which implies analyticity of the (generally off-shell) correlation function (
15
) at fixed real
(p_{2}+p_{3})^{\mu}
when
a positive-timelike imaginary part is added to
p_{3}^{\mu}
:

\mathcal{R}(p_{3},p_{2})\mbox{ is analytic in }D\equiv\{(p_{2},p_{3})~|~(p_{2}+p_{3})^{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{1,3}\mbox{ and }{\rm Im}\,p_{3}^{\mu}\in V^{+}\}\,,

(21)

where
V^{+}\equiv\{p^{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{1,3}~|~p^{0}>|\vec{p}|\}
is the set of
positive-timelike vectors.

Equations (
20
) and (
21
)
are the building blocks from which one would like to establish crossing symmetry. Before moving on, it is instructive to highlight two important points:

(i)

For
2\to 2
scattering, the amplitude (
15
) is a function of the two independent Mandelstam invariants

s=-(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad t=-(p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}\,.

(22)

Using
\mathcal{A}=a_{1}^{\dagger}
,
\mathcal{D}=b_{4}
, and the stability condition mentioned earlier,
(
20
) simplifies to

\mathcal{R}(s,t)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{}_{\rm out}\langle 34|\mathbbm{1}|12\rangle_{\rm in}&\mbox{$s$-channel kinematics}\,,\\
-{}_{\rm in}\langle 24|\mathbbm{1}|13\rangle_{\rm out}&\mbox{$u$-channel kinematics}\,.\end{array}\right.

(23)

The opposite arrangements of “in” and “out” states in (
23
) explains why fixed-
t
analyticity
connects the
s
-channel amplitude
to the
complex conjugate
of the
u
-channel amplitude.

(ii)

At face value, the statements (
20
) and (
21
) have non-overlapping validity.
This is the well-known difficulty in establishing crossing: the axiomatic domain
D
does not intersect the mass shell.
In fact, it is simply not possible to add a small timelike imaginary part to a real momentum
without leaving the mass shell:

{\rm Im}\,p_{3}^{\mu}\in V^{+}\quad\implies\quad{\rm Re}\,p_{3}\cdot{\rm Im}\,p_{3}\neq 0\quad\implies\quad p_{3}^{2}\neq-m_{3}^{2}\in\mathbb{R}\,.

(24)

The traditional “work-around” involves two steps
Bros:1965kbd
.
First, we consider off-shell correlators as a function of
s
and complexified masses

-p_{i}^{2}\mapsto m_{i}^{2}+\xi
, where
\xi\in\mathbb{C}
. For
2\leftarrow 2
scattering, by writing

s=m_{3}^{2}+m_{4}^{2}-2p_{3}{\cdot}p_{4}+2\xi
, one sees that (
21
) contains an off-shell domain of the form

D\supset D_{1}\equiv\{s,m_{3}^{2}\in\mathbb{C}~|~{\rm Im}\,s>0,\,{\rm Re}\,\xi<\xi_{0}<0\}\,,

(25)

where
\xi_{0}
is fixed by the masses and the kinematics in the transverse plane (see App.
A
). Next, we need to show that the on-shell limit is sufficiently mild for amputated correlators such as
\mathcal{R}
, and
specifically that they enjoy
local analyticity
in a neighborhood of the mass shell
for real physical momenta:

D_{2}\equiv\{s\in\mathbb{R}~|~|s|>s_{0}\}\times\{\xi\in\mathbb{D}_{r}(\xi_{0})\}\,.

(26)

Here,
\mathbb{D}_{r}(\xi_{0})
denotes an open disk centered at
\xi_{0}<0
with radius
r
large enough for the disk to contain the mass shell (the origin in the
\xi
-plane:
\xi=0
).
Then, general properties of complex functions of two variables imply that the analyticity domain
D_{\mathcal{R}}
of
\mathcal{R}
contains the mass shell as well as complex
s
, at least for sufficiently large
s
. To put it more clearly, we have

D_{\mathcal{R}}\supset D_{1}\cup D_{2}~\implies~D_{\mathcal{R}}\supset\{s\in\mathbb{C}~|~{\rm Im}\,s>0,\;\mbox{$|s|$ ``large enough'' and}~\xi=0\}\,.

(27)

For the reader’s benefit, this mathematical step is reviewed at a physicist’s level of rigor in App.
A
. The upshot is that crossing paths like those in Fig.
3
exist
and remain on shell at all times.
To our knowledge, such arguments have been carried out rigorously for
2\leftarrow 2
scattering processes but have never been completed for generic
n\leftarrow m
processes (excluding the
3\leftarrow 2
case
Bros:1985gy
).

The central objective of this paper is to address and resolve point
(i)
for
n
-point processes and to formulate a reasonable statement of crossing in the general case. We propose to take seriously the idea that the two objects in (
23
) (or more generally in (
20
)) are related by an on-shell analytic continuation, and leave a rigorous proof addressing point
(ii)
to future work.

3
Crossing symmetry

In this section, we introduce the
crossing equation
(
33
), which relates asymptotic observables of the type discussed above.

3.1
Main proposal: Crossing two particles in an
n
-point amplitude

To state our proposal precisely, it is useful to introduce a complex variable
z
, which naturally generalizes the
s
-plane to
n
-point kinematics. We first go to the Lorentz frame in which the lightcone components of the momenta
p_{2}
and
p_{3}
are real and directly opposite, i.e.,
p_{3}^{\pm}=-p_{2}^{\pm}
. Next, we apply the deformation parameter
z
, such that

\displaystyle p_{2}^{\mu}(z)=\big(\phantom{+}zp_{2}^{+},\,\phantom{+}\tfrac{1}{z}p_{2}^{-},\,p_{2}^{\perp}\big)\,,

(28)

\displaystyle p_{3}^{\mu}(z)=\big({-}zp_{2}^{+},\,{-}\tfrac{1}{z}p_{2}^{-},\,p_{3}^{\perp}\big)\,,

where
p_{2}^{\pm}<0
.
It is straightforward to verify that momentum conservation
\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(z)=0
and on-shell conditions
p_{i}(z)^{2}=p_{i}^{2}
are preserved for any complex value of
z
.

Owing to point
(ii)
mentioned earlier, we only expect crossing to work for “large enough”
z
. Indeed, to avoid extraneous terms
in (
20
),
z
needs to be sufficiently large
that
|zp_{i}^{+}|>|p_{j}^{+}|
for all
i\in\{2,3\}
and
j\in A\cup D
, where
A
and
D
denote the sets of particles created and annihilated within the
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{D}
strings respectively.
We will consider paths that take the form of large arcs across the
z
half-plane:

z
-1
1

(29)

The Mandelstam invariants that involve both
2
and
3
simultaneously, or neither of them, remain fixed. On the other hand, the invariants that get deformed are of the form
s_{ijk\ldots}
with
i\in\{2,3\}
and
j,k,\ldots\in A\cup D
,

s_{ijk\ldots}(z)=-(p_{i}(z)+p_{j}+p_{k}+\ldots)^{2}=z\,p^{+}_{i}(p^{-}_{j}+p^{-}_{k}+\ldots)+\mathcal{O}(z^{0})\,,

(30)

and hence for large enough
z
, they rotate counter-clockwise and remain within one half-plane, from being large positive to large negative or vice versa. Our proposal is that such paths
indeed connect the two observables in (
20
), as was shown in Fig.
3
.
We summarize it in the following relation:

\left[\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,b_{3}a_{2}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle\right]_{{\curvearrowleft}z}=-\langle 0|\mathcal{D}\,a_{2}b_{3}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{A}|0\rangle\,.

(31)

We call (
31
) the
crossing equation
. Its simplest instance is when
\mathcal{A}=\prod_{i\in A}a_{i}^{\dagger}
gives a multi-particle incoming state and
\mathcal{D}=\prod_{i\in D}b_{i}
creates a multi-particle outgoing state. Before the continuation, this choice results in the ordinary time-ordered scattering amplitude
S_{D3\leftarrow 2A}
. The crossing equation in this case can be written as

\left[S_{D3\leftarrow 2A}\right]_{{\curvearrowleft}z}=\left[\langle D|a_{3}Sa_{2}^{\dagger}|A\rangle\right]_{{\curvearrowleft}z}=-\langle D|Sa_{2}S^{\dagger}a_{3}^{\dagger}S|A\rangle=-\sumint_{X,Y}S_{D\leftarrow Y}S^{\dagger}_{Y2\leftarrow 3X}S_{X\leftarrow A}\,,

(32)

where on the right-hand side we inserted two resolutions of identity. In the diagrammatic language, we have

2
3
S
A
D
cross
{{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}2}\leftrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}3}}
\bar{3}
\bar{2}

(33)

Here, red color-coding marks which particles are being crossed. If they carried charges, after crossing
2

and

.
The more general case (

and

contain both connected and disconnected terms.

This is the main proposal which we will explore in this paper, for both massive and massless particles.
To be fully precise, our conjecture is that this holds whenever the retarded product is analytic in a neighborhood of the mass shell, meaning that there is no obstruction from point
(ii)
above. This condition is non-trivial and a tentative criterion is proposed in Sec.
6
.

Spinning particles

Let us emphasize that the above proposal can also be straightforwardly stated for amplitudes of spinning particles, even though all our examples will involve only scalars. All that is needed is to deform the external polarization spinors and vectors in such a way that the transverse conditions (
p_{j}{\cdot}\varepsilon_{j}(z)=0
) and/or the Dirac equation (
(\not{p}_{j}(z)-m_{j})u_{j}(z)=0
) remain satisfied at all times.
Since the deformations in (
28
) coincide with a boost along the 3-direction, a simple way to achieve this is to apply the same boost to the polarizations of all particles
j\in B\cup C
, which gives, respectively, for vectors and spinors:

Alternatively, one could view spinning amplitudes as collections of scalar amplitudes multiplying suitable polarization structures, but note that this approach can introduce extra branch cuts

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{j}^{\mu}(z)

(34)

\displaystyle u_{j}(z)

(35)

It might sound strange that crossing has something to say about tree-level amplitudes, which are rational functions.
The point is that amplitudes are really boundary values of (sums of) analytic functions and so, under crossing, they can contain

\delta
-function contributions. Below, we wish to check whether these are also correctly reproduced.
For this reason, it is important to carefully keep track of the
i\varepsilon
factors.

In (
35
), we can omit the
i\varepsilon
prescription for
s_{13}
since this invariant is spacelike in the considered kinematics and, consequently, its propagator cannot vanish. However, we need to keep
i\varepsilon
for the timelike Mandelstam invariant
s_{45}
.
We now analytically continue the kinematics so as to
swap the energies of particles 2 and 3.
The invariant
s_{13}
starts negative and rotates in the counter-clockwise direction, which means it ends up below the positive axis, while the invariant
s_{45}
stays fixed:

s_{ij}
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}s_{45}}
{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}s_{13}}

(36)

The result of analytic continuation can be written as

\left[i\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}\right]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[-1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{13}}=\frac{-ig^{3}}{(-s_{45}+M^{2}-i\varepsilon)(-s_{13}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon)}\,,

(37)

where now
s_{13}>0
and its
-i\varepsilon
prescription matters.
Notice how the second propagator ended up with the “wrong”
i\varepsilon
prescription. This fact is significant because this pole is accessible in
245\leftarrow 13
kinematics.
5
5

5

Strictly speaking, the pole cannot be exactly on the real axis since
M
must be a resonance — obviously, if
M
can be kinematically produced, it can decay.
However, in the narrow-width approximation this does not affect the present calculations:
the two-particle cut near resonance is proportional to

2{\rm Re}\left(\frac{-i}{-s_{45}+M^{2}-iM\Gamma}\right)\approx 2\pi\delta(-s_{45}+M^{2})+\mathcal{O}(\Gamma)\,.

(38)

A more detailed discussion can be found in
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
.

This is a similar situation to how the crossing transformation for
34\leftarrow 12
scattering ends up on the “wrong side” of the
u
-channel branch cut for a general non-perturbative amplitude (see Fig.
1
).
Here, however, the
s_{45}
pole is still on the correct side, so we cannot identify the right-hand side with a complex conjugated amplitude.
It is a different object
.

The crossing equation in (
33
) gives a definite prediction for the result of analytic continuation. It should be equal to the complex-conjugated five-particle amplitude, plus a non-linear term where the heavy particle
M
is produced, namely

\displaystyle\left[i\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}\right]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[-1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{13}}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}i\mathcal{M}^{{\dagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}+[i\mathcal{M}_{45\leftarrow M}]\,2\pi\delta(-s_{45}+M^{2})\,[i\mathcal{M}^{{\dagger}}_{M2\leftarrow 13}]

(39a)

\displaystyle=\frac{-ig^{3}}{(-s_{45}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon)(-s_{13}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon)}+\frac{2\pi\delta(-s_{45}+M^{2})g^{3}}{-s_{13}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon}

(39b)

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{-s_{45}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon}+2\pi i\delta(-s_{45}+M^{2})\right)\frac{-ig^{3}}{-s_{13}+M^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,.

(39c)

Using the familiar identity
\frac{1}{x\pm i\varepsilon}=\text{PV}\frac{1}{x}\mp i\pi\delta(x)
, this agrees precisely with (
37
)! Diagrammatically:

(40)

Note that a cut through the
s_{13}
propagator is not allowed, because it does not fit in the pattern (
33
).

It is easy to verify that the proposal (
33
) also works for any other
3\leftarrow 2
tree diagram:
\mathcal{M}^{{\dagger}}
gives the correct continuation of the amplitude except for propagators involving
s_{45}
, which stays fixed during the rotation.
Indeed, after the rotation and with
z
still large, the only timelike invariants are
s_{13}
,
s_{24}
,
s_{25}
and
s_{45}
. The first three rotate counter-clockwise and end up below the axis, as appropriate for
\mathcal{M}^{{\dagger}}
. Propagators involving
s_{45}
, however, do not get complex conjugated, and this is fixed by the
S
blob (which is only different from identity where
\delta(-s_{45}+M^{2})
has support).

We conclude that the proposed crossing relation in (
33
) is the simplest option that is not obviously disproved by tree-level considerations.
A proposal which would not get the correct
i\varepsilon
’s at tree level would stand no chance of landing on the correct branch for the more intricate functions that appear at loop level.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{gathered}

(41)

Here (as always in this paper) time flows from right to left and we use an all-outgoing convention for the momenta.
The amplitude is given by

i\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}\ell}{\pi^{2}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{13})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell+p_{45})^{2}-i\varepsilon]}\,,

(42)

where we use the conventions that vertices in the Feynman diagram corresponding to
i{\cal M}
come with a factor of
(-i)
, the propagator of an edge with momentum
q_{e}
is taken to be
\frac{-i}{q_{e}^{2}+m_{e}^{2}-i\varepsilon}
, and we multiply by an overall factor of
(-1)^{\text{V}}
where
V
is the total number of vertices. These factors of
i
contribute
i^{-\text{L}}
to
{\cal M}
.
The expression in (
42
) can easily be evaluated to be

\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}=\frac{-2}{s_{13}(z-\bar{z})}\left[\mathrm{Li}_{2}(z)-\mathrm{Li}_{2}(\bar{z})+\frac{1}{2}\left(\log z+\log\bar{z}\right)\left(\log(1-z)-\log(1-\bar{z})\right)\right],

(43)

where we have introduced two independent variables
z
and
\bar{z}
, which relate to kinematic variables as follows

z\bar{z}=\frac{s_{26}}{s_{13}}\quad\text{and}\quad(1-z)(1-\bar{z})=\frac{s_{45}}{s_{13}}\,.

(44)

The formula (
43
) is valid in the Euclidean region
R^{\text{E}}
described below.
Different kinematic regions can be obtained by continuations in
z
and
\bar{z}
.
Due to the symmetry in
z\leftrightarrow\bar{z}
, we can take
\bar{z}<z
without loss of generality. The branch points of the amplitude are at
z=0
,
z=1
and
z=\infty
, as well as the corresponding
\bar{z}=0
,
\bar{z}=1
and
\bar{z}=\infty
. Moreover, there is a branch point at
z=\bar{z}
.
We can separate the different kinematic regions in the space of
z
and
\bar{z}
according to the signs of the invariants
s_{26}
,
s_{45}
and
s_{13}
, as follows:

(45)

where the regions are labeled with a superscript of the Mandelstam invariants that are positive. For example,
R^{(26)}
is the region in
(z,\bar{z})
where
s_{26}>0
,
s_{45}<0
and
s_{13}<0
, which corresponds to
0<z<1
and
\bar{z}<0
. We have labeled the Euclidean region, where the invariants are either all positive or all negative, as
R^{\text{E}}
. When two invariants are positive, we have the relation
R^{(13)(45)}=R^{(26)}
, and its permutations.

When computing the amplitude in any other kinematic region than the one where
0<z,\bar{z}<1
, we must specify the imaginary parts of
z
and
\bar{z}
to land on the correct branches of the polylogarithms in (
43
). Using that the signs of the imaginary parts of the invariants can be implemented as
s_{ij}\to s_{ij}+i\varepsilon
, we get the following assignments of infinitesimal imaginary parts of
z
and
\bar{z}
for the scattering amplitude
\mathcal{M}
:

\displaystyle z

\displaystyle\to z+i\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad\bar{z}\to\bar{z}-i\varepsilon\qquad\text{in }\quad R^{(26)}\,,\quad R^{(45)}\,,\quad R^{(26)(45)}\,,

(46a)

\displaystyle z

\displaystyle\to z-i\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad\bar{z}\to\bar{z}+i\varepsilon\qquad\text{in }\quad R^{(13)}\,,\quad R^{(13)(45)}\,,\quad R^{(13)(26)}\,.

(46b)

The crossing of particles
2
and
3
starting from
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}

will provide a first non-trivial example of the crossing equation at loop level. Let us start by working out the result of the rotation via (
29
). During the crossing step, both
s_{26}
and
s_{13}
rotate in a large semicircle in the lower half-plane to become timelike. The corresponding rotation of
z
and
\bar{z}
is achieved with
z
rotating clockwise around
1
and
\bar{z}
fixed,

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{gathered}

(47)

After the rotation, we end up with the amplitude in the region
0<\bar{z}<z<1
, in addition to the discontinuity across the branch cut that starts at
z=1
. Since the amplitude and the complex amplitude are the same in this region, we can write the result of the crossing as

\left[\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{13}}\\
{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{26}}\end{subarray}}=\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}+\text{Disc}_{z>1}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\,,

(48)

where
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}
is given by the expression in (
43
), and the discontinuity across the branch cut at
z>1
is defined as
\text{Disc}_{z>1}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}=\left.\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\right|_{z+i\varepsilon}-\left.\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\right|_{z-i\varepsilon}
, which we compute to be

\text{Disc}_{z>1}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}=\frac{-2\pi i}{s_{13}(z-\bar{z})}\log\frac{z}{\bar{z}}\,,

(49)

for
z>1
and
s_{13}<0
.

Next, we compare this result with the prediction from the crossing equation in (
33
). After crossing, the physical channel will be the one in which
1
and

The prediction is therefore that the amplitude after the rotation should be equal to the conjugated amplitude plus a cut in the
s_{45}
channel, both of which are computed in the region
2456\leftarrow 13
:

\left[\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{13}\\
\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{26}\end{subarray}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}\,,

(53)

where cut operation
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}
is defined through the rightmost picture in (
3.3
).
6
6

6

In general, by
\mathrm{Cut}(i{\cal M})
we denote the result of replacing all cut propagators according to
\frac{-i}{q_{e}^{2}+m_{e}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\to 2\pi\delta^{\pm}(q_{e}^{2}+m_{e}^{2})
and complex-conjugating all the vertices and propagators in the
S^{\dagger}
blob, where the
\pm
signs are selected according to the energy flow. In the conventions explained below (
42
) and after absorbing the overall minus sign on the right-hand side of the crossing equation (
33
), the overall factors of
i
in
\mathrm{Cut}\,\mathcal{M}
work out to be
-i^{-\text{L}_{L}+\text{L}_{M}-\text{L}_{R}-1}
, where
\text{L}_{L}
,
\text{L}_{M}
, and
\text{L}_{R}
are the number of loops in the left, middle, and right blobs respectively.

To verify this prediction, we compute the cut as

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}=-\left(2\pi\right)^{2}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}\ell}{i\pi^{2}}\frac{\delta^{-}[\ell^{2}]\delta^{+}\big[(\ell+p_{45})^{2}\big]}{(\ell-p_{13})^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,,

(54)

where the momentum labelings were given in (
41
).
We work in the center-of-mass frame of
s_{45}
, where momentum conservation and the delta functions impose

\ell^{0}=\ell^{0}_{\ast}=-\frac{[s_{13}(1-z)(1-\bar{z})]^{1/2}}{2}\,,

(55)

as well as

p_{13}^{0}=\frac{s_{13}(z+\bar{z}-2)}{2[s_{13}(1-z)(1-\bar{z})]^{1/2}}\quad\text{and}\quad|\vec{p}_{13}|=\frac{z-\bar{z}}{2}\left[\frac{s_{13}}{(1-z)(1-\bar{z})}\right]^{1/2}\,.

(56)

Putting all this together, we get

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}=-i\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\cos\theta}{s_{13}-2\ell^{0}_{\ast}(p_{13}^{0}-|\vec{p}_{13}|\cos\theta)}=\frac{-2\pi i}{s_{13}(z-\bar{z})}\log\frac{z}{\bar{z}}\,.

(57)

Comparing the last expression with (
48
) validates (
53
), in accordance with the prediction of the crossing equation in (
33
).

Figure 4
:
Paths of analytic continuation prescribed by unitarity and crossing.
Top:
The dashed green path is the one prescribed by unitarity. Note that
\bar{z}
stays fixed both when evaluating the unitarity equation and during the crossing path. The red path is the one prescribed by crossing, and it immediately enters the second sheet upon the start of the analytic continuation.
Bottom:
Unitarity path and crossing path for the process
456\leftarrow 123
in the region
R^{(13)(45)}
. In this region,
\bar{z}<0
,
0<z<1
and we take
\bar{z}\to\bar{z}+i\varepsilon
. The crossing path prescribes a rotation in
\bar{z}
to have a positive imaginary part on the second sheet, and
z
rotates clockwise around
1
, into a new kinematic channel
R^{(26)(45)}
.

In the triangle example above, we can compare the result with what we could have predicted using unitarity. Unitarity would tell us that the imaginary part of the amplitude in a given kinematic channel is equal to the sum over all cuts in that channel. For the triangle diagram above, unitarity gives

2i\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}=\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}-\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri \textdagger}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{all allowed}\\
i,j\end{subarray}}\mathrm{Cut}^{\text{U}}_{s_{ij}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\,.

(58)

We warn the reader that the definition of “Cut” here is subtly but consequentially different from the one used before. The unitarity cuts (or “Cutkosky-rules” cuts) in (
58
) instruct us to complex conjugate the amplitude to the right of the cut
Cutkosky:1960sp
. We denote this fact with a superscript “
U
” standing for “unitarity cut”. As can be deduced from (
46a
), the difference between the amplitude and its conjugate in this case is simply given by the difference between
\mathcal{M}
evaluated at
z+i\varepsilon
and
z-i\varepsilon
. Furthermore, the only allowed cut in the
3456\leftarrow 12
kinematics is the one in the
s_{45}
channel. That is, the left-hand side of (
58
) is simply given by the discontinuity across the branch cut at
z>1
:

\disc_{z>1}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}=\mathrm{Cut}^{\text{U}}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}_{3456\leftarrow 12}\qquad\text{(unitarity prediction)}\,.

(59)

Since the unitarity cut happens to agree with
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}
up to a sign, this is the same prediction as we obtained using the crossing equation in (
48
). However, the paths that led to this are different, as we have shown in Fig.
4
(top). The unitarity path takes us between the value of
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}
above and below the branch cuts, while staying entirely on the first sheet in the
z
-plane. Note that
\bar{z}
remains fixed along both the unitarity and crossing paths. On the other hand, the crossing path immediately enters the second sheet of the
z
-plane at the beginning of the analytic continuation. In this example, it is easy to see that despite the different paths, the analytic continuation of the cut is straightforward and the crossing path can simply be extended to a full circle. As a result, (
59
) simply becomes a consistency condition for the crossing prediction. We emphasize that, despite arriving at this conclusion, the two paths are conceptually different.

The story changes if we instead compare crossing and unitarity in a kinematic channel where more than one cut is allowed, as shown in Fig.
4
(bottom). Unitarity tells us to compare
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}
on the first sheet, above and below the branch cut in
\bar{z}
, which leads to

2i\mathrm{Im}\,\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{456\leftarrow 123}=\mathrm{Cut}^{\text{U}}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}_{456\leftarrow 123}+\mathrm{Cut}^{\text{U}}_{s_{13}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}_{456\leftarrow 123}\qquad\text{(unitarity prediction)}\,,

(60)

where, as usual, the right-hand side of the cut is given by conjugated Feynman rules. The crossing prediction, however, is

\left[\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{245\leftarrow 136}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{26}\\
\scalebox{1.05}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{13}\end{subarray}}=\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri \textdagger}}_{345\leftarrow 126}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{345\leftarrow 126}\qquad\text{(crossing prediction)}\,.

(61)

To avoid clutters, we leave implicit in this formula that
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}
should be evaluated with the middle part between the orange cuts in Fig.
4
conjugated. Note that the endpoint of the crossing path corresponds to an
i\varepsilon
prescription in
z
and
\bar{z}
that cannot be represented by any of the choices in (
46a
) and (
46b
). This reflects rather explicitly the fact that the object obtained through crossing is
not
a conventional time-ordered amplitude.

There are two things to note about the result in (
61
). First, the crossing prediction is not equivalent to the one obtained by unitarity, and it is not obvious how to connect the two. Second, if we can compute the amplitude in different kinematic regions, the crossing equation gives a new way to predict the
individual
cut contribution
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}
in this channel: it corresponds to the difference between
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri \textdagger}}_{345\leftarrow 126}
(i.e.,
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}
with
\bar{z}\to\bar{z}+i\varepsilon
and
z\to z-i\varepsilon
) and
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}
with
\bar{z}\to\bar{z}+i\varepsilon
and
z\to z+i\varepsilon
. In this case, this cut is not equal to the total discontinuity in the kinematic region
R^{(26)(45)}
, since the discontinuity would also include contributions from cuts in the
s_{26}
channel. The crossing equation, therefore, yields a prediction distinct from that of total discontinuities in a kinematic channel, underpinning some of the recent developments regarding the relation between cuts and discontinuities
Abreu:2014cla
;
Bourjaily:2020wvq
. In this example, it is perhaps not surprising that the
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}
operation is equivalent to taking the discontinuity in
z>1
, as we found in the region where
0<\bar{z}<1
. The non-trivial information we get from the crossing equation, however, is which branches we land on, since the cut
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{345\leftarrow 126}
generally has non-vanishing real and imaginary parts.

All-loop predictions

We can extend our previous discussion to a prediction of the
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}
operation to the
L
-loop triangle ladder diagram, whose full expression is given by
Usyukina:1993ch

\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri ladder}}=\frac{(-1)^{L}}{L!(z{-}\bar{z})}\frac{1}{s_{13}s_{45}^{L{-}1}}\sum_{j=L}^{2L}\frac{\left(-1\right)^{j}j!\left[\log z{+}\log\bar{z}\right]^{2L{-}j}}{\left(j{-}L\right)!\left(2L{-}j\right)!}\left[\text{Li}_{j}(z)-\text{Li}_{j}(\bar{z})\right]\,,

(62)

and the analytic continuations in
z
and
\bar{z}
given in (
46a
) and (
46b
).

Starting in the region
R^{(13)(45)}
, we cross
2\leftrightarrow 3
and end in the region
R^{(26)(45)}
with
0<z<1
and
\bar{z}<0
.
The prediction of the crossing equation is exactly analogous to the one for the one-loop triangle: the analytically continued amplitude should be equal to the conjugated amplitude plus the cuts in the
s_{45}
channel, namely

where the middle part between the orange cuts is conjugated as before.

In this case, individual cuts in the
s_{45}
channel are not straightforward to compute. Instead of checking the crossing equation, we can use it to make a non-trivial prediction: namely that the sum of cuts on the right-hand side of (
3.4
) is equal to the discontinuity across the
z>1
branch cut of (
62
), while keeping
\bar{z}<0
fixed above the branch cut (i.e., taking
\bar{z}\to\bar{z}+i\varepsilon
):

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{all cuts}\\
\text{in }s_{45}\end{subarray}}\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri ladder}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\frac{(-1)^{L}\left(s_{45}\right)^{1-L}}{L!s_{13}(z-\bar{z})}\sum_{j=L}^{2L}\frac{\left(-1\right)^{j}j!\left(\log(-z\bar{z})+i\pi\right)^{2L-j}}{\left(j-L\right)!\left(2L-j\right)!}\frac{2\pi i\log^{j-1}z}{(j-1)!}\,.

(66)

The
i\pi
’s in this expression represent the non-trivial prediction of the crossing equation. More generally, the crossing equation computes
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}
, including taking into account which branches we land on. Of course, the prediction (
66
) is admittedly not too surprising either since the calculation amounted to taking an
s_{45}
discontinuity. The interesting aspect of the method is that it explains clearly
how
to take the discontinuity even in situations that are not controlled by unitarity (this cut is not equal to the imaginary part of the amplitude).

In Sec.
5
, we will further test the crossing equation in numerous additional loop-level examples.

3.5
Conjectural extension: Crossing multiple particles?

Let us now discuss our conjecture for a generalization of the crossing equation to crossing multiple particles at the same time. For concreteness, we start with the process
CD\leftarrow AB
, where each of
A
,
B
,
C
, and
D
is a non-empty set of particles. We then cross the clusters
B
and
C
.
In light-cone coordinates, the analytic continuation is described by the following deformation of the momenta for each particle in the
B
and
C
clusters:

\displaystyle p_{b}^{\mu}(z)=\big(zp_{b}^{+},\,\tfrac{1}{z}p_{b}^{-},\,p_{b}^{\perp}\big)\quad\text{for all }b\in B\,,

(67)

\displaystyle p_{c}^{\mu}(z)=\big(zp_{c}^{+},\,\tfrac{1}{z}p_{c}^{-},\,p_{c}^{\perp}\big)\quad\text{for all }c\in C\,,

where
p^{\pm}_{b}<0<p^{\pm}_{c}
and
-p_{i}^{2}=p_{i}^{+}p_{i}^{-}-(p_{i}^{\perp})^{2}
.
The on-shell conditions are preserved.
Moreover, in order for momentum conservation to remain satisfied along the deformation, we work in any Lorentz frame in which the condition

\sum_{b\in B}p^{\pm}_{b}+\sum_{c\in C}p^{\pm}_{c}=\sum_{a\in A}p^{\pm}_{a}+\sum_{d\in D}p^{\pm}_{d}=0\,,

(68)

is satisfied. Note that, by Lorentz invariance, we could equally have
deformed the momenta for the clusters
A
and
D
, i.e., the

B\leftrightarrow C
and
A\leftrightarrow D
crossing paths are equivalent. We perform the same deformation along a large arc in the
z
plane as illustrated previously in (
29
). Only the Mandelstam invariants
s_{I}
for which
I
and its complement
\bar{I}
both contain at least one label from
B\cup C
and one from
A\cup D
get
z
-deformed. They behave as
s_{I}(z)\sim z
at large
z
. For example, if
s_{I}
starts off timelike (
s_{I}>0
), it rotates along a large arc in the upper half-plane to being spacelike (
s_{I}<0
).

Equation (
33
) gives our main conjecture for the crossing of
two
elementary (stable) particles. However, as noted above that equation, the path which crosses two stable particles
b\leftrightarrow c
is equivalent to one which crosses the conjugate clusters
A\leftrightarrow D
, for any number of legs.
We can use this observation to motivate a simple candidate crossing equation valid for arbitrary clusters of particles
A,B,C
and
D
. We simply tack an
S
blob onto each cluster:

S
B
A
C
D
cross
{{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}B}\leftrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}C}}
-
S^{\dagger}
S
S
S
S
\bar{C}
A
\bar{B}
D
Y
X
Z
W

(69)

In terms of an equation, this translates to

\left[S_{CD\leftarrow AB}\right]_{{\curvearrowleft}z}=-\sumint_{X,Y,Z,W}S_{B\leftarrow Z}S_{D\leftarrow Y}S^{\dagger}_{YZ\leftarrow XW}S_{W\leftarrow C}S_{X\leftarrow A}\,.

(70)

Once again, a more general version of this crossing conjecture can be obtained by embedding (
69
) in a larger blob diagram.
The two-particle crossing equation in (
33
) is obtained as special case
where
B
and
C
are single-particle states, so that we can ignore the
S
blocks acting on them, thanks to the stability condition.

From the viewpoint of local field theory, the multi-particle extension of the crossing equation (
69
)
is somewhat mysterious, since the disconnected products of
S
blobs cannot be obtained from
the LSZ reduction of any correlation function (which would necessarily involve a chain of
S
’s as in Sec.
2
).
Nonetheless, we will find in Sec.
4
that it passes very non-trivial checks at tree level. However, in Sec.
6.5
, we are going to discuss a one-loop example with massless kinematics in which the conjecture (
69
) meets an analytic obstruction due to an anomalous threshold.

3.6
Webs of observables

At this stage, we can ask whether every observable can be related to any other using the above crossing rules.
Surprisingly, we find that the answer turns out to be no already for
n=5
. This is illustrated in the diagrams in Fig.
5
, where a pair of observables is joined if and only if it participates in the same crossing relation.

We recall from
(
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, Tab. 1)
that there are
2
and
8
measurement types for
n=4
and
5
respectively. Crossing moves for
n=4
only relate amplitudes to complex-conjugated amplitudes. For
n=5
, there are two separate families with
4
measurement types each. For example,
S_{2\leftarrow 3}
turns out to be connected to
S_{3\leftarrow 2}
by a composition of two crossing moves, but
S_{2\leftarrow 3}
and
S^{\dagger}_{2\leftarrow 3}
are not.

For
n=6
particles, there are 28 measurement types according to
the classification in
Caron-Huot:2023vxl
, but
the more speculative relation (
69
) adds four new objects
(the two at the ends of the middle panel top line in Fig.
6
and their complex conjugates),
for a total of 32. They split into four families: with
4
,
8
,
8
, and
12
entries each, as shown in Fig.
6
.

Notably, we find that
S_{4\leftarrow 2}
,
S_{2\leftarrow 4}
, and
S_{3\leftarrow 3}
all lie in the same family, but their complex conjugates do not. Also, our crossing relations do not seem to relate the
inclusive cross sections (leftmost diagram in the first family) to the amplitude. We find this somewhat surprising since some relations of this kind have been discussed in the 1970s in the context of Regge theory (see
(
Brower:1974yv
, Ch. 6)
).
We stress that we are solely using the specific analytic continuation encoded by the crossing equations (
33
) and its possible extension (
69
), and that
there might exist other ones reconnecting the families.

Finally, let us note that it is also interesting to consider how crossing relates conventional time-ordered amplitudes with different labels
(not just measurement types). For example, one may be interested in relating different channels of the same diagram. This will be discussed and exemplified further near the end of Sec.
5
, and we anticipate that such relations between kinematics could be useful in the context of differential equation approaches to Feynman integrals, alleviating the need to separately compute initial conditions in each channel
chicherin:2020oor
.

.

), whereas the dashed lines display the three-particle crossing using (

).

Crossing a single particle

Note that a single particle cannot be crossed to become its own anti-particle with one deformation because such a deformation would violate momentum conservation. However, we can achieve it by a composition of multiple crossing moves described above. First, notice that because of the symmetry of (
69
), its right-hand side can be alternatively obtained by starting with the process
AD\leftarrow BC
and crossing
A\leftrightarrow B
instead. In equations,

\left[S_{AD\leftarrow BC}\right]_{\scalebox{1.05}{$\curvearrowleft$}z^{\prime}}=-\sumint_{X,Y,Z,W}S_{B\leftarrow Z}S_{D\leftarrow Y}S^{\dagger}_{YZ\leftarrow XW}S_{W\leftarrow C}S_{X\leftarrow A}\,,

(71)

where the analytic continuation is obtained by deforming the momenta of particles
A
and
B
instead of
B
and
C
with a complex parameter
z^{\prime}
, just as in (
67
). This is a different continuation from that used in (
70
). But by combining these two crossing moves, we obtain a two-leg path of continuation between
S_{CD\leftarrow AB}
and
S_{AD\leftarrow BC}
. In the
n=4
case, it is the path described in the original work of BEG
Bros:1965kbd
: it starts from the
s
-channel, passes through the
u
-channel (from the wrong side of branch cuts) in the intermediate step, and then lands on the
t
-channel. Let us introduce the following shorthand notation:

S_{CD\leftarrow AB}\;\xrightarrow[(B,C);\;(A,\bar{B})]{\text{cross}}\;S_{\bar{A}D\leftarrow B\bar{C}}\,,

(72)

for this analytic continuation. For later convenience, we will additionally keep track of which labels correspond to anti-particles by adding bars. For example,
B
is a particle on the right-hand side because it was crossed an even number of times, but
\bar{A}
and
\bar{C}
are anti-particles because they got crossed an odd number of times.

Let us now isolate a single particle
n
and divide the remaining ones into four non-empty sets
I
,
J
,
K
,
L
, such that we are dealing with the amplitude
S_{KLn\leftarrow IJ}
. We then use the following chain of the above moves
Mizera:2021fap
:

S_{KLn\leftarrow IJ}\;\xrightarrow[(J,KL);\;(I,\bar{J})]{\text{cross}}\;S_{n\bar{I}\leftarrow J\bar{K}\bar{L}}\;\xrightarrow[(\bar{L},n);\;(J\bar{K},L)]{\text{cross}}\;S_{\bar{I}\bar{J}K\leftarrow\bar{L}\bar{n}}\;\xrightarrow[(\bar{n},\bar{I}\bar{J});\;(\bar{L},n)]{\text{cross}}\;S_{KL\leftarrow\bar{n}IJ}\,.

(73)

The scattering amplitude on the right-hand side is
S_{KL\leftarrow\bar{n}IJ}
, which differs from the starting point of the continuation only by the fact that the outgoing particle
n
is now an incoming anti-particle
\bar{n}
.

For amplitudes with planar ordering
(IJKLn)
, it is known perturbatively that there are no anomalous thresholds in any of the six upper half-planes involved in this deformation, which means that (
73
) can be established rigorously
Mizera:2021fap
. In other cases, (
73
) depends on the validity of the crossing conjecture (
70
).

4
Tree-level proof of the cluster crossing equation

In this section, we prove the crossing conjecture (
69
) for an arbitrary scalar
n
-point tree-level diagram. In our conventions, the amplitude for such a diagram in the channel
CD\leftarrow AB
is given by

i\mathcal{M}_{CD\leftarrow AB}=(-ig)^{|\mathcal{E}|+1}\prod_{I\in\mathcal{E}}\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,,

(74)

where the product runs over the set
\mathcal{E}
of all internal edges in the diagram, and
I
denotes the set of external momenta which enter that edge of the tree. To avoid clutter, we have taken the coupling constant for every vertex to be the same (labeled with
g
); the generalization to arbitrary coupling constants is trivial. Paralleling the discussion in Sec.
3.5
, a similar proof can be constructed diagram-by-diagram for non-scalar scattering amplitudes after gauge fixing.

Of course, since tree amplitudes are rational functions of momenta made by multiplying simple ingredients (propagators and vertices), it is obvious that the expressions in different kinematics all admit closely related expressions. The non-trivial thing we will check is that the
i\varepsilon
’s work out precisely as predicted by (
69
).

Applying the kinematic deformation from Sec.
3.1
, the set of Mandelstam invariants
s_{I}=-p_{I}^{2}
appearing in a given diagram partitions into those that do depend on the deformation parameter
z
and those that do not. Let us call the two sets
\mathcal{Z}
and
\mathcal{N}
respectively. The set
\mathcal{Z}
consists of those
s_{I}
such that
I
and its complement
\bar{I}
both contain at least one label from the crossed sets
B,C
and at least one from the fixed set
A,D
. In those situations,
p_{I}^{+}\sim z
and
p_{I}^{-}\sim 1
, such that the corresponding Mandelstam invariant is deformed as
s_{I}\sim z
.
The set
\mathcal{N}
contains all remaining invariants, which are
z
-independent since they have either
p_{I}^{\pm}\sim z^{\pm 1}
or
p_{I}^{\pm}\sim 1
.

The analytic continuation illustrated in (
29
) has the effect that all
s_{I\in\mathcal{Z}}
either start spacelike and rotate to become timelike with wrong-sign
-i\varepsilon
, or start timelike and rotate to become spacelike in which case their
i\varepsilon
is no longer needed. The tree-level amplitude (
74
) therefore crosses to

\big[i\mathcal{M}_{CD\leftarrow AB}\big]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}\mathcal{Z}}=(-ig)^{|\mathcal{N}|+1}(ig)^{|\mathcal{Z}|}\prod_{I\in\mathcal{N}}\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\prod_{J\in\mathcal{Z}}\frac{i}{-s_{J}+m_{J}^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,,

(75)

where we have denoted with
|\mathcal{N}|
and
|\mathcal{Z}|
the total numbers of invariants in the sets
\mathcal{N}
and
\mathcal{Z}
, respectively.
To condense this expression, we have not distinguished between spacelike and timelike edges, since
\pm i\varepsilon
can be freely added to the spacelike ones anyway with no effect.

The goal is now to prove the crossing conjecture (
69
).
To this end, we have to sum over all possible ways of placing the vertices of the tree into the form (
69
), and compare the answer with the explicit result obtained in (
75
). Before diving into the full proof, we start with a simple example that illustrates the intuition.

4.1
Simple example revisited

Let us circle back to the example from Sec.
3.2
, and show how the crossing relation works out for the diagram

i\mathcal{M}_{1}+i\mathcal{M}_{2}=\frac{-ig^{3}}{(-s_{45}+m_{45}^{2}-i\varepsilon)(-s_{13}+m_{13}^{2}+i\varepsilon)}=\left[i\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{13}\\
\scalebox{1.05}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{12}\end{subarray}}\,.

A

B

C
and
D
in (
69
). A cut going through an external line does not affect it, since it is already on-shell.

(83)

However, the left diagram is not allowed by the factorization of the blobs in (
69
) (the
S
factors must separately act within
A
,
B
,
C
and
D
, and consequently, the rightmost vertex must be on the left of the first cut). The right diagram vanishes by conservation of momentum flow in the
p^{-}
components.

In fact, there is yet another reason why neither of them is allowed: the red-blue line can actually never be cut, as we will show in Sec.
4.3
. One can check that no placements of vertices are allowed apart from the ones spelled out in (
80
) and (
81
). We have therefore proven that the crossing equation (
70
) holds for this diagram.

4.2
Classification into red and blue edges

Armed with the insight from this simple example, we now turn to proving crossing for any tree diagram. As we just saw, it is useful to look at momentum conservation for the
p^{+}
and
p^{-}
components separately, both to determine which edges can potentially go on-shell, and also to exclude diagrams that are not allowed by momentum conservation in each component separately. We therefore use the same red and blue labeling as in the previous example, which gives us a simple way to exclude many of the cut diagrams that naively seem to fit into (
69
).

As before, for any tree diagram, let us label the edges that have
p_{I}^{+}\sim z
in red,
p_{I}^{-}\sim 1
in blue, as
z\to\infty
. Any given edge might be red (dashed), blue (solid), red-blue, or remain uncolored (black/dotted) if its momentum does not satisfy the aforementioned scaling. In the absence of a black edge, an example diagram looks like

(84)

We notice some additional features of this classification. First, the set of red edges
\mathcal{R}
must be connected by itself thanks to momentum conservation. It also needs to be connected to all external particles in the set
B\cup C
.
Likewise, the set of blue edges
\mathcal{B}
is a tree connected to
A\cup D
. We have therefore established that the original tree diagram contains a connected red tree
\mathcal{R}
, and a connected blue tree
\mathcal{B}
:

(85)

We can further ask if the red and blue trees are edge-disjoint or not. Let us consider the first case,
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}=\varnothing
. It means that there might have been some black edges, but by momentum conservation, they could not be connected to any of the external legs. We conclude that there could be at most
one
such black edge. Let us call it
e
. Moreover, it needs to be spacelike at large
z
, since the momentum flowing into it has
p_{e}^{+}\sim 1
and
p_{e}^{-}\sim z^{-1}
.

The remaining possibility is that
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\varnothing
with the intersection
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
consisting of all the red-blue edges. The set of red-blue edges needs to be a tree by itself. If it was not, it would have at least two disconnected components. Such components could then be connected by a combination of a purely-red path and a purely-blue path, which would necessarily form a loop:

(86)

Therefore, since the diagram we started with is a tree, the number of connected components of
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
needs to be one, i.e., it has to be a tree by itself.

In the rest of this section, we focus on the second case, since the first one will be entirely analogous.

4.3
Absence of cuts through red-blue edges

Next, we would like to show that cuts through red-blue edges are always disallowed by kinematic considerations. As the simplest non-trivial example, consider the following diagram:

d
c
c
b
b
b
c
a

(88)

Here,
a\in A
,
b\in B
, etc.
Denoting the momentum running through the red-blue edge as
p
, and setting
s=-p^{2}
as the kinematic invariant and
m
as the mass of the edge, the amplitude is
i\mathcal{M}=\frac{-i(-ig)^{2}}{-s+m^{2}-i\varepsilon}
. Depending on the momenta,
s
can be either positive or negative, and the energy flow in the red-blue edge can be either positive or negative.

The amplitude after crossing
s
from spacelike to timelike becomes

[i\mathcal{M}]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s}=\frac{-i(-ig)^{2}}{-s+m^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,.

(89)

To compare this result with the crossing equation, we draw and compute all diagrams that are consistent with (
69
):

Naively, it looks like the sum of all of these contributions to the crossing conjecture is

[i\mathcal{M}]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}i(-ig)^{2}\left[\frac{1}{-s+m^{2}+i\varepsilon}+2\pi i\delta(s)-2\pi i\delta(s)+2\pi i\delta(s)\right]=\frac{-i(-ig)^{2}}{-s+m^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,,

(92)

which would not agree with the answer in (
89
). When writing (
92
), we have, however, ignored one crucial restriction: the positive-energy flow across the orange cuts. In all of the diagrams above except the first one, the red-blue edge is forced by momentum conservation to have a negative and large
p^{-}
component. If
p^{+}
is positive, this means that
s
must be spacelike, and if
p^{+}
is negative, then positive energy flow across the cuts cannot be satisfied, since the energy of the edge is proportional to
p^{+}{+}p^{-}
. In either case, we conclude that the red-blue edge cannot be cut.

This argument generalizes to bigger diagrams: a spectator from the set
A
or
C
cannot attach in any of the
S
blobs on the left-hand side of (
69
), and vice versa for spectators from
B
and
D
. Say
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
was contained in one of the
S
blobs, for example the top-left one shown in the diagram below:

\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}\neq\varnothing:\hskip 28.45274pt

Then, there would need to be at least one blue line with energy flowing backwards across the unitarity cut, as shown in the figure, since factorization forbids the red-blue tree to contain only outgoing blue edges.
This possibility is excluded by momentum conservation in the
p^{-}
components. In conclusion, the full red-blue tree
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
must be fully contained inside the
S^{\dagger}
blob. By the same logic, we conclude that if the diagram instead has a black edge, it must be within
S^{\dagger}
.

4.4
Factorization into branches

To summarize, we now have the following classification of all edges in a general tree diagram: they are either red, blue, red-blue or black. The red-blue ones can never be on-shell, and hence they cannot be cut in the crossing equation. In addition, there can at most be one black edge in the tree, and it must be spacelike by momentum conservation, so it also cannot be cut and must be within
S^{\dagger}
. Looking back at (
75
), we see that the edges that always remain within the
S^{\dagger}
blob in the crossing conjecture (
69
), are precisely the ones in the set
\mathcal{Z}
, and rotate to become past timelike, i.e., with a propagator
\frac{-i}{-s_{J}+m_{J}^{2}+i\varepsilon}
. However, the edges which are either red, blue, or black are in the set
\mathcal{N}
and do not rotate under crossing. Hence, we arrive at the following classification for a generic tree-level diagram:

\mathrm{{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}red}},\,\mathrm{{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}blue}},\mathrm{black\ edges}\in\mathcal{N}\quad\text{and}\quad\text{{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}red}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}blue} edges}\in\mathcal{Z}\,.

(94)

The sets
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{Z}
are equal. Thus, the second product in (
75
) is accounted for and we are left with explaining how to obtain the first product from the crossing conjecture.

What remains is to figure out how the red and blue edges can fit into the blob pattern (
69
). To this end, let us look at the original diagram after removing all the black and red-blue edges:
