(95)

This procedure introduced a number of vertices (leaves of
\mathcal{R}\cap\mathcal{B}
or
e
), which we denoted with white circles. Following the previous discussion, white vertices have to belong to
S^{\dagger}
, while the remaining vertices can be in either of the blobs.

We are going to view each of the disconnected components as a separate tree, for which a momentum
q
is injected via the white vertex in
S^{\dagger}
. In fact, we can treat the red and blue parts separately. We call each such component a
branch
. Since the tree diagram factorizes into a part that always stays within
S^{\dagger}
, as well as a number of branches, the final step of the proof involves proving crossing at the level of each branch separately.

4.5
Proof of crossing for each branch

In this last step of the proof of crossing at tree level, we consider a single branch of the tree, where momentum is injected through a single white vertex in
S^{\dagger}
. Each individual branch is independent of the deformation parameter
z
, and therefore we are left with proving an equality between two quantities, which we will show using unitarity. We can represent the contribution from each branch separately, i.e., the contribution where an off-shell momentum
q
is injected into a part of the diagram, via a form factor
F(q)
in this theory. Matrix elements of the form factor between some states
X
and
Y
are given by

iF_{Y\leftarrow X}(q)={}_{\text{out}}\langle Y|i\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)|X\rangle_{\text{in}}=i\langle Y|S\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)|X\rangle\,,

(96)

where
\mathcal{O}_{F}
is a local operator. We remind the reader that the discussion in this section applies diagram by diagram in gauge-fixed perturbation theory.

It is simple to work out how the Mandelstam invariants rotate for a branch: since all the propagators in the diagram belong to either the set
A\cup D
or
B\cup C
, i.e., the set
\mathcal{N}
, meaning that all of the Mandelstam invariants remain fixed during crossing, and its contribution is equal to:

iF^{\mathrm{branch}}_{D\leftarrow A}=(-ig)^{|\mathcal{E}_{\text{branch}}|+1}\prod_{I\in\text{branch}}\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,,

(97)

where we have labeled the part of the tree amplitude originating from the branch with
F
. Note that since
B
and
C
do not appear in this equation, crossing them is trivial. So, to prove the crossing equation for a single branch, we have to show that the sum over all contributions that fit into the blob pattern of (
69
) simply results in
iF^{\mathrm{branch}}_{DB\leftarrow CA}
, as if the only contribution were that from a single
S
blob.

To evaluate the prediction of crossing from (
69
), we consider a blue branch without loss of generality, i.e., one whose external particles belong to either
A
or
D
. When the sets
B
and
C
are crossed, the kinematics of the branch remain unchanged. The multi-particle crossing proposal predicts

\left[iF^{\mathrm{branch}}_{D\leftarrow A}\right]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}\mathcal{Z}}=i\sumint_{X,Y}\langle D|S|Y\rangle\langle Y|\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)S^{\dagger}|X\rangle\langle X|S|A\rangle\,,

(98)

where we have used that
iF^{\dagger}_{Y\leftarrow X}(q)={}_{\text{in}}\langle Y|i\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)|X\rangle_{\text{out}}=i\langle Y|\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)S^{\dagger}|X\rangle
. Note that we have incorporated the minus sign from (
70
) into the factors of
i
. This equation can be evaluated straightforwardly with unitarity, using that the sum is over complete sets of states
|X\rangle
and
|Y\rangle
, to give

\left[iF^{\mathrm{branch}}_{D\leftarrow A}\right]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}\mathcal{Z}}=i\langle D|S\mathcal{O}_{F}(q)|A\rangle=iF^{\mathrm{branch}}_{D\leftarrow A}\,.

(99)

(100)

Comparing this result with (
97
), we see that the crossing proposal and the explicit computation agree for the crossing if the tree diagram contains a single branch.

It only remains to make sure that the crossing proposal for multi-particle crossing (
69
) reproduces the correct overall sign in cases where the tree diagram contains multiple branches.
If we note that the crossing equation for branches, (
100
) does not introduce an extra sign for the white vertex
v
, so we can combine the findings in this section to write the prediction of (
69
) as

\big[i\mathcal{M}_{CD\leftarrow AB}\big]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}\mathcal{Z}}=(-ig)^{|\mathcal{N}|+|\mathcal{Z}|+1}\prod_{I\in\mathcal{N}}\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\prod_{J\in\mathcal{Z}}\frac{-i}{-s_{J}+m_{J}^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,,

(101)

where
\mathcal{N}
is the set of invariants
s_{I}
that appear in this diagram and stay fixed during crossing, while
\mathcal{Z}
is the set of those that rotate. Note that
|\mathcal{N}|+|\mathcal{Z}|+1
is the total number of vertices in the diagram. The minus sign in front is the one from the right-hand side of (
69
). This expression agrees with (
97
), thus concluding the proof.

Before concluding this section, let us make the comment that we could have proven (
100
) at the level of individual diagrams using the largest-time equation
tHooft:1973wag
;
Veltman:1994wz
, which involves summing over all possibilities of the vertices being distributed between
S
and
F^{\dagger}
. As an example of how such an argument works out, we focus on the simplest diagram of a branch with only one propagator and show how (
100
) works in perturbation theory. We have to show that there are non-trivial cancelations between the different ways of distributing the vertices of the branch into the crossing equation. We consider a branch with large minus components of all momenta (a blue branch), without loss of generality. To manifest the cancelation between different terms, we add and subtract diagrams for which
q
attaches in the leftmost
S
-blob as follows:

(102c)

In equations, the top line is given by

\displaystyle iF^{\text{branch}}

\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}-2\pi\Theta(-q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})-2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})

(103a)

\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,.

(103b)

Note that we only have modified the top line (
102a
) by a trivial zero: we added and then subtracted all the diagrams for which the vertex of the branch is in the
S
-blob on the left. This was not a random choice. Indeed, the diagrams are now organized in a way that makes manifest cancellations between them.
In particular, the diagrams
1
,
2
,
4
and
6
, which have the rightmost
S
shaded in blue, cancel. This follows from unitarity: their sum precisely corresponds to all ways of distributing the two vertices between the
S
on the left, and
F^{\dagger}
in the middle region; in equations,

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}1}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}2}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}4}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}6}

\displaystyle=\frac{-i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}-i\varepsilon}-2\pi\Theta(-q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})

(104a)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt+\frac{i}{-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2}+i\varepsilon}-2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})=0\,.

(104b)

This type of cancellation between placements of vertices between
S
and
S^{\dagger}
is familiar from perturbative proofs of the cutting rules using the largest-time equation
7
7

7

These proofs often using a black-and-white-vertex notation (nothing to do with our black/white coding) to show how diagrams, their conjugates and cuts cancel among each other, see e.g.
Veltman:1994wz
. When mapping those proofs to our setup, the vertices in the leftmost
S
blob would be white, and the vertices in the middle
S^{\dagger}
blob would be black. The sum over all configurations of black and white vertices cancel among each other.
.
Similarly, diagrams
3
and
5
cancel, since they correspond to all ways of distributing the white vertex between
S
and
S^{\dagger}
, keeping the black vertex fixed in the rightmost
S
blob (shaded in red with diagonal lines):

{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}3}+{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}5}=-2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})+2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})=0\,.

(105)

Last, keeping the white vertex in the leftmost
S
blob, represented with the grey dotted region, shows that diagrams
7
and
8
cancel:

{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}7}+{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}8}=-2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})+2\pi\Theta(q^{0})\delta(-s_{I}+m_{I}^{2})=0\,.

(106)

The only remaining contribution is diagram 9, which corresponds to placing the whole diagram within the
S
blob with an extra overall minus sign, which is precisely what we expect from (
97
), and agrees with (
103b
).

As a final remark, notice that since this proof of the crossing equation for branches presented in this subsection is based on unitarity, we never actually used that the diagram was a tree. Thus, we have also proven the crossing equation (
33
) in the case of diagrams in which two particles attach to the rest of the diagram at a single vertex, and those two particles are precisely the ones that are crossed from incoming to outgoing.

5
One-loop crossing for massless five-point amplitudes

In this section, we verify the crossing conjecture for all massless one-loop master integrals relevant for (up to) five-point functions in dimensional regularization around
\mathrm{D}=4
dimensions. In doing so, we will employ various techniques to evaluate the master integrals and their cuts, including Schwinger parameters, the embedding space formalism, and differential equations.

For fully massless amplitudes, non-trivial crossings start at four points, where amplitudes simply analytically continue to complex-conjugated amplitudes using the crossing path (
67
). Below, we will illustrate through a concrete example that this well-established conclusion is, indeed, in perfect harmony with our crossing equation (
33
).

At five points, there is only one possibility for crossings of the process
S_{345\leftarrow 12}
: we cross an incoming particle with an outgoing one.
8
8

8

At five point, the option of crossing an incoming particle (e.g., 2) with a cluster of two particles (e.g., 34) is not considered separately because it is equivalent to a single particle crossing (e.g., crossing 1 and 5).
Taking these two particles to be 2 and 3, this leads to

\begin{gathered}\hbox{\raise-77.51114pt\hbox{\resizebox{}{}{{\hbox{{\hbox to180.25pt{\vbox to77.51pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 45.9342pt\lower-20.45938pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 66.93}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

(107)

In what follows, we will meticulously check the consistency of this statement against explicit examples. In particular, at the end of this section, we will have checked all possible crossings for up to five-point diagrams, and up to pentagon topology.

Note that at one loop, non-trivial crossings begin with massless bubbles. Indeed, tadpoles either vanish (when massless) or are functions of the mass in the loop (when massive). Consequently, they remain unchanged under crossing and are not considered here.

Finally, towards the end of this section, we will explore further applications of crossing symmetry, such as how it can be used in practical calculations to relate time-ordered amplitudes with different labels.

5.1
Bubbles

We start by establishing crossing for massless bubble integrals, which in
\mathrm{D}
spacetime dimensions are given by

\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\text{bub}}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell+p)^{2}-i\varepsilon]}\,.

(108)

This integral is easy to perform; it evaluates to

\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\text{bub}}=\frac{\Gamma\big(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-1\big)^{2}\Gamma\big(2-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\big)}{\Gamma(\mathrm{D}-2)}(p^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}\,.

(109)

Here,
p^{2}
corresponds to the squared momentum entering the vertices, which at five points can be realized by four different configurations (up to permutations of indices):

(110)

When crossing particles
2
and
3
, the relevant rotations for each of the four diagrams above are summarized as

s_{ij}
{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}s_{12}}

s_{ij}
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}s_{23}}

s_{ij}
{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}s_{13}}

s_{ij}
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}s_{45}}

(111)

Since each bubble amplitude depends on a single invariant
s_{ij}
, it is clear that in the case of the first three diagrams, for which the relevant invariant
s_{ij}
either ends up negative or on the wrong side of the cut (for
s_{13}
), the amplitudes analytically continue to complex conjugated amplitudes. There is no possible cut in the
s_{45}
channel in these cases, so this prediction is consistent with the expectation from (
107
), since the
S
-blob is necessarily trivial.

In the case of the fourth diagram, the amplitude is unchanged under the rotation. The prediction from the crossing equation in (
107
) is that we get the conjugated amplitude plus a cut in the
s_{45}
channel, namely

(112)

The right-hand side is a sum over the conjugated amplitude and the unitarity cut, so the two contributions sum up to the amplitude
\mathcal{M}_{542\leftarrow 13}^{\text{bub}}
. The easiest way to see this explicitly is by noticing that the cut term in (
112
) is a unitarity cut (or Cutkosky cut), so it is equal to twice the imaginary part of the amplitude. Therefore,

\mbox{RHS of \eqref{eq:bubCross}}=\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\text{bub}\dagger}+2\text{Im}\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\text{bub}}=\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\text{bub}}\,,

(113)

and the direct computation agrees with the crossing prediction from (
107
).

In fact, an analogous argument also holds for crossing any clusters of particles for any two-point Feynman diagram by unitarity. Indeed, both evaluate to the same class of functions; by dimensional analysis, one has

(115)

along with all permutations of the external legs.
The amplitude in loop-momentum space is given by

\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{13})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell+p_{45})^{2}-i\varepsilon]}\,,

(116)

which evaluates to

\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{tri}}=\frac{\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)^{2}}{\Gamma\left(\mathrm{D}-3\right)}\frac{(-s_{13}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}-(-s_{45}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}}{s_{45}-s_{13}}\,.

(117)

This expression is valid in any physical kinematic region, and the
i\varepsilon
’s are needed only if the corresponding
s_{ij}>0
. Note that this expression is invariant under placing
\pm i\varepsilon
in the denominator since the numerator makes corrections proportional to
\varepsilon
at
s_{45}=s_{13}
.

Let us check the crossing equation (
107
) when crossing particles
2
and
3
in
345\leftarrow 12
kinematics, i.e., starting in the region where
s_{13}<0<s_{45}
. The result of crossing is

\left[\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{tri}}\right]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[-1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{13}}=\frac{\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)^{2}}{\Gamma\left(\mathrm{D}-3\right)}\frac{(-s_{13}+i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}-(-s_{45}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}}{s_{45}-s_{13}+i\varepsilon}\,.

(118)

107
), we have to compute the conjugated amplitude and the cut in
s_{45}
channel, according to

(119)

In an equation, this reads

\left[\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{tri}}\right]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[-1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{13}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{245\leftarrow 13}\,,

(120)

where the cut term on the right-hand side is defined by the rightmost picture in (
119
). The conjugated amplitude
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
is easily obtained from (
117
), and the cut is given by

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{245\leftarrow 13}=-\left(2\pi\right)^{2}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{\delta^{-}[\ell^{2}]\delta^{+}\big[(\ell+p_{45})^{2}\big]}{(\ell-p_{13})^{2}+i\varepsilon}\,.

(121)

The calculation of the cut term proceeds analogously to the
s_{45}
cut of the six-point triangle diagram from Sec.
3.3
, with the modifications that we now take one external leg to be massless and work in
\mathrm{D}
dimensions instead of four.
We define
\ell^{0}_{\ast}\equiv-\frac{\sqrt{s_{45}}}{2}
as the value of
\ell^{0}
and
|\vec{\ell}|
imposed by the delta functions. After performing the two delta functions, we can write the cut in spherical coordinates as

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}=-\frac{i\Omega_{\mathrm{D}-2}}{2\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}}\left(\frac{s_{45}}{4}\right)^{\frac{\mathrm{D}-4}{2}}\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{(1-\cos^{2}\theta)^{\frac{\mathrm{D}-4}{2}}\mathrm{d}\cos\theta}{s_{13}-2\ell^{0}_{\ast}(p_{13}^{0}-|\vec{p}_{13}|\cos\theta)-i\varepsilon}\,,

(122)

where
\Omega_{d}=\frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2)}
is the solid angle of a sphere in
d
-dimensions. In the center-of-mass frame of
s_{13}
, we have

p_{13}^{0}=-\frac{s_{45}+s_{13}}{2\sqrt{s_{45}}}\quad\text{and}\quad|\vec{p}_{13}|=-\frac{s_{45}-s_{13}}{2\sqrt{s_{45}}}\,,

(123)

such that

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{2456\leftarrow 13}=\frac{2\pi is_{45}^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)}{(s_{45}-s_{13}+i\varepsilon)\Gamma(\mathrm{D}-3)}\,.

(124)

Using the identity

(-s_{45}+i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}-(-s_{45}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}=\frac{2\pi i}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)}s_{45}^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}\,,

(125)

where we have assumed that
s_{45}>0
, we get

\begin{split}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri}}_{245\leftarrow 13}&=\frac{\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)^{2}}{\Gamma\left(\mathrm{D}-3\right)(s_{45}-s_{13}+i\varepsilon)}\\
&\hskip-85.35826pt\times\left[(-s_{13}+i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}-(-s_{45}+i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}+\frac{2\pi i}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)}s_{45}^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}\right]\\
&\hskip-85.35826pt=\frac{\Gamma\left(3-\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{2}-2\right)^{2}}{\Gamma\left(\mathrm{D}-3\right)}\frac{(-s_{13}+i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}-(-s_{45}-i\varepsilon)^{\mathrm{D}/2-2}}{s_{45}-s_{13}+i\varepsilon}\,,\end{split}

(126)

where an
i\varepsilon
can be freely added to
\mathcal{M}^{\text{tri\textdagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
, as explained below (
117
). This result agrees with the one obtained by crossing in (
118
), thus verifying the crossing equation for this diagram. Other kinematic channels can be checked analogously.

(127)

The corresponding amplitude is given by

\mathcal{M}_{34\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{1})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{12})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{123})^{2}-i\varepsilon]}\,,

(128)

with
p_{i}^{2}=0
,
-p_{12}^{2}=s
and
-p_{23}^{2}=t
. We also define
-p_{13}^{2}=u
. The physical
s
-channel is defined using
s>0
,
t<0
,
u<0
, and the
t
and
u
channels are defined analogously by symmetry. Therefore, we can check the crossing relations between any two of these kinematic regions.

In the Euclidean region (corresponding to the
u
-channel where
s<0
and
t<0
), the integral in (
128
) evaluates to
Bern:1993kr

\mathcal{M}_{34\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^{+}}\frac{C(\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}st}\Big[(-s)^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{1}\pm i\varepsilon\right)\\
+(-t)^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{2}\mp i\varepsilon\right)\Big]\,,

(129)

in
\mathrm{D}=4-2\epsilon
. Here,
C(\epsilon)=\frac{2\Gamma(1-\epsilon)^{2}\Gamma(\epsilon+1)}{\Gamma(1-2\epsilon)}
and the variables
z_{1}
and
z_{2}
are given in terms of the kinematic invariants as

z_{1}=1+\frac{s}{t}\quad\text{and}\quad z_{2}=1+\frac{t}{s}\,.

(130)

Note that in the kinematic regions where
\frac{s}{t}>0
, the
i\varepsilon
in the hypergeometric functions are arbitrary as long as they have opposite signs, resulting in a continuous function in the region where
s<0
and
t<0
.

In the
s
- and
t
-channel kinematic regions, the amplitude is given by (
129
) after the replacements
(-s)^{-\epsilon}\to(-s-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}
and
(-t)^{-\epsilon}\to(-t-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}
, respectively. Whenever
s
and
t
have opposite signs, the
i\varepsilon
in the hypergeometric functions are not needed. The
i\varepsilon
-prescriptions are summarized in Tab.
1
.

The crossing relations for the massless box are straightforward to establish. For a
2\leftarrow 2
process, we are only allowed to cross two particles thanks to stability. We start by looking at crossings starting in the
u
-channel region, where
s<0
and
t<0
. We can, for example, cross particles
2
and
3
, which rotates
s
to be timelike with a negative imaginary part. During the rotation, the hypergeometric functions in (
129
) remain on their principal sheet, and after rotation the
i\varepsilon
for
z_{1}
and
z_{2}
will not play any role

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{gathered}

(131)

Moreover, the prefactor
(-s)^{-\epsilon}
will rotate to become
(-s+i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}
, so the
u
-channel amplitude has rotated to the conjugated
s
-channel amplitude

\left[\mathcal{M}_{24\leftarrow 13}^{\mathrm{box}}\right]_{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\curvearrowleft$}s}=\mathcal{M}_{34\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}\dagger}\,.

(132)

Similarly, we obtain the rotations from the
u
-channel to the
t
-channel by symmetry. We note that for purely massless
2\leftarrow 2
scattering, there is no mass scale on which a corner cut could depend on, resulting in the vanishing of the box
p_{i}^{2}
-cut for all
i

(
Abreu:2017ptx
, Eq. (4.20))
. Thus, equation (
132
) (as well as its
u
- and
t
-channel analogues) agrees with the crossing-equation prediction.

Next, let us check crossing when starting in the
s
-channel (
s>0
,
t<0
and
u<0
). In this channel, the amplitude is given by (
129
) after replacing
(-s)^{-\epsilon}\to(-s-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}
. After the analytic continuation, we get
z_{1}\to z_{1}-i\varepsilon
and
z_{2}\to z_{2}+i\varepsilon
,

, the resulting expression is, once again, the complex-conjugated amplitude

All other crossing relations are obtained by symmetry.

(135)

It is defined by the expression

\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{1})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{12})^{2}-i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{123})^{2}-i\varepsilon]}\,,

(136)

with
p_{i}^{2}=0
,
-p_{45}^{2}=s_{45}
,
-p_{12}^{2}=s_{12}
and
-p_{23}^{2}=s_{23}
.
The integral was computed exactly in
\mathrm{D}=4-2\epsilon
spacetime dimensions in
Bern:1993kr
;
Kozlov:2015kol
and can be written as a sum of hypergeometric functions

\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\frac{C(\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}s_{12}s_{23}}\big[(-s_{12})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}^{A}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{1}\right)+(-s_{23})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}^{A}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{2}\right)\\
-(-s_{45})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}^{A}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{3}\right)\big]\,,

(137)

with
C(\epsilon)
defined below (
129
). Here, the variables
z_{1}
,
z_{2}
and
z_{3}
are given in terms of the kinematic invariants as

z_{1}=1-\frac{s_{45}-s_{12}}{s_{23}}\,,\qquad z_{2}=1-\frac{s_{45}-s_{23}}{s_{12}}\,,\qquad z_{3}=1-\frac{(s_{45}-s_{12})(s_{45}-s_{23})}{s_{12}s_{23}}\,.

(138)

Note that despite the dependence on
\epsilon
, which makes the equation more concise, (
137
) is valid in any spacetime dimension. Above, we have used the superscript
A
to denote that the branch of the hypergeometric functions must be specified and it depends on the kinematic region, as discussed in detail below.

Signs of the imaginary parts of
z_{i}
for the amplitude in different kinematic regions. All other physical channels are obtained by relabeling symmetry and/or time reversal. A bullet “
\bullet
” denotes that no
i\varepsilon
-prescription is needed. If an imaginary part is listed for a specific region, there may still be subregions in which it is superfluous since the corresponding
z_{i}<0
, but we still include it to avoid further subdivisions. The conjugated amplitude is obtained by flipping the signs of all
i\varepsilon
. The entries with
\pm i\varepsilon
mean that one can choose either, as long as one is consistent.

To get the correct expression in different kinematic regions, we must be careful to be on the correct side of the branch cuts of the hypergeometric functions in (
137
). In the Euclidean region carved by
s_{12}<0
,
s_{23}<0
and
s_{45}<0
, we can get the correct form by using the real values:
\,{}_{2}F_{1}^{A}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{i}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\pm}\,{}_{2}F_{1}^{A}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{i}\pm i\varepsilon\right)
. Equivalently, we can assign
+i\varepsilon
and
-i\varepsilon
to the
z_{i}
such that the discontinuities vanish, which requires the two hypergeometric functions with
z_{i}>1
to have opposite
i\varepsilon
.
This follows from the formula for the discontinuity of the hypergeometric function:

\displaystyle\disc_{z>1}[_{2}F_{1}(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon,z)]

\displaystyle\equiv\,_{2}F_{1}(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon,z+i\varepsilon)-\,_{2}F_{1}(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon,z-i\varepsilon)

(139a)

\displaystyle=-2\pi i\epsilon z^{\epsilon}\Theta(z-1)\,,

(139b)

which gives that the discontinuity of
\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}
in each
z_{i}
is equal and given by

\disc_{z_{i}>1}\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\frac{2\pi iC(\epsilon)}{\epsilon s_{12}s_{23}}\,\left(-\frac{s_{45}}{z_{3}}\right)^{-\epsilon}\Theta(z_{i}-1)\,.

(140)

In the kinematic region where
s_{45}<s_{23}<0
and
s_{45}<s_{12}<0
, we can see from (
138
) that
z_{i}<1
for all
i
such that the amplitude does not have any branch cuts coming from the hypergeometric functions. Therefore, we can unambiguously write, when
s_{45}<s_{12},s_{23}<0
,

\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}=\frac{C(\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}s_{12}s_{23}}\big[(-s_{12})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{1}\right)+(-s_{23})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{2}\right)\\
-(-s_{45})^{-\epsilon}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{3}\right)\big]\,.

(141)

We will use this expression to analytically continue to other kinematic regions. Note that it is not sufficient to simply take
s_{ij}\to s_{ij}+i\varepsilon
for the invariants that are positive; the function is written in a form that requires more care to match the correct Feynman
i\varepsilon
prescription. A list of the
i\varepsilon
prescriptions needed for the
z_{i}
in each region is given in Tab.
2
. The analytic continuation of the prefactors is simply
(-s_{ij})^{-\epsilon}\to(-s_{ij}-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}
for
s_{ij}>0
.

Crossing prediction

To show that the crossing equation (
107
) holds, we need to check it for the crossing of any pair of particles, between any allowed kinematic regions. While we present only one example in detail, we have checked, using analogous computations, that the crossing equation holds for any other crossing channels.

As an example, we start in
345\leftarrow 12
kinematics, in the region
s_{23}<0<s_{45}\ll s_{12}
, and cross particles
2
and
3
. This places us in the region
245\leftarrow 13
. In the first kinematic region, one can check that the amplitude is simply given by substituting
s_{12}\to s_{12}+i\varepsilon
and
s_{45}\to s_{45}+i\varepsilon
into (
141
). The crossing results in
s_{12}
becoming large and negative, while
s_{23}
and
s_{45}
stay fixed. After the analytic continuation, we end up in the region
s_{12}\ll s_{23}<0<s_{45}
with
z_{1}\to z_{1}-i\varepsilon
and
z_{2}\to z_{2}+i\varepsilon
. This is summarized below:

(142)

According to Tab.
2
, the expression we end up with has the same
i\varepsilon
prescriptions for the
z_{i}
’s as
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}{\dagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
. Therefore, the analytically continued amplitude differs from
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}{\dagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
by a discontinuity of the prefactor
(-s_{45})^{-\epsilon}
, which is given by

\disc_{s_{45}>0}(-s_{45})^{-\epsilon}=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^{+}}\left[(-s_{45}-i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}-(-s_{45}+i\varepsilon)^{-\epsilon}\right]=2i\sin(\pi\epsilon)s_{45}^{-\epsilon}\,.

(143)

Putting everything together, we have, after the analytic continuation in
s_{12}
,

\left[\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}\right]_{\scalebox{1.05}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{12}}=\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}{\dagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}-\underbracket{\frac{2iC(\epsilon)\sin(\pi\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}s_{12}s_{23}s_{45}^{\epsilon}}\,_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon,1-\epsilon;z_{3}\right)}_{\Delta\mathcal{M}}\,.

(144)

Based on the crossing equation (
107
), the continued amplitude should be equal to the inclusive amplitude

\left[\mathcal{M}_{345\leftarrow 12}^{\mathrm{box}}\right]_{\scalebox{1.05}{$\curvearrowleft$}s_{12}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}{\dagger}}_{245\leftarrow 13}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}\,.

(145)

Therefore, to establish the crossing relation, we need to check whether the expression for the inclusive amplitude obtained by analytic continuation agrees with a direct computation. When comparing (
144
) with (
145
), one sees that this check amounts to verifying that the cut in the
s_{45}
channel equals the difference between
\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
and its complex-conjugate, namely to check if

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\Delta\mathcal{M}\,.

(146)

We now proceed to compute the cut
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}
to show that this formula is indeed true.

Cut computation

The cut integral is defined by

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}=-(2\pi)^{2}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{\delta^{-}(\ell^{2})\delta^{+}[(\ell-p_{123})^{2}]}{[(\ell-p_{1})^{2}+i\varepsilon][(\ell-p_{12})^{2}+i\varepsilon]}\,.

(147)

To compute this integral, we use the
embedding space formalism
described in
Abreu:2017ptx
;
Abreu:2017mtm
, which allows us to rewrite the
C
-particle cut of a
\mathrm{D}
-dimensional
n
-gon as an
(n-|C|+1)
-gon in
(\mathrm{D}-|C|)
dimensions. We review the arguments in App.
B
.
In doing so, we end up with an integral with kinematics resembling a lower-dimensional triangle integral. In Schwinger-parameter space, it is given by

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}=-\frac{2iC(\epsilon)\sin(\pi\epsilon)}{s_{45}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\alpha}{\mathrm{GL}(1)}\alpha_{0}^{-1-2\epsilon}\\
\times\left[-\alpha_{0}\alpha_{1}\left(\frac{s_{12}}{s_{45}}-1\right)-\alpha_{0}\alpha_{2}\left(\frac{s_{23}}{s_{45}}-1\right)-\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\left(-\frac{s_{12}s_{23}}{s_{45}}\right)+\frac{1}{s_{45}}\alpha_{0}^{2}\right]^{\epsilon-1}\,.

(148)

Its kinematic dependence resembles a triangle integral with one internal mass:

(149)

We can directly evaluate the integral in (
148
) by gauge fixing the
\mathrm{GL}(1)
symmetry to set
\alpha_{0}=1
, before performing the remaining integrals over
\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}
. We find

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}=-\frac{2iC(\epsilon)}{\epsilon s_{45}^{\epsilon}}\Bigg[\frac{\pi}{s_{12}s_{23}}\left(-\frac{(s_{12}+s_{23}-s_{45})s_{45}}{s_{12}s_{23}}\right)^{\epsilon}\\
+\frac{\sin(\pi\epsilon)}{(1+\epsilon)(s_{45}-s_{12})(s_{45}-s_{23})}\,_{2}F_{1}\Big(1,1;2+\epsilon;\frac{s_{12}s_{23}}{(s_{45}-s_{12})(s_{45}-s_{23})}\Big)\Bigg]\,.

(150)

In the kinematic region we end up in after crossing (
s_{12}\ll s_{23}<0<s_{45}
), we can rewrite (
150
) as

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{45}}\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{box}}_{245\leftarrow 13}=-\frac{2iC(\epsilon)\sin(\pi\epsilon)}{\epsilon^{2}s_{12}s_{23}s_{45}^{\epsilon}}\,_{2}F_{1}\big(1,-\epsilon;1-\epsilon;z_{3}\big)\,,

(151)

thanks to the hypergeometric identity

{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(1,1;2+\epsilon;\frac{s_{12}s_{23}}{(s_{45}-s_{12})(s_{45}-s_{23})}\Big)=\frac{(s_{45}-s_{12})(s_{45}-s_{23})}{s_{12}s_{23}}\frac{1+\epsilon}{\epsilon}\,\\
\times\left[\,{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(1,-\epsilon;1-\epsilon;z_{3}\Big)-\frac{\pi\epsilon}{\sin(\pi\epsilon)}\left(-\frac{(s_{12}+s_{23}-s_{45})s_{45}}{s_{12}s_{23}}\right)^{\epsilon}\right]\,.

(152)

The result in (
151
) matches perfectly with the crossing prediction made in (
146
).

A midway summary

So far, we have checked the crossing equation for, essentially, all massless one-loop topologies in
\mathrm{D}=4-2\epsilon
up to boxes. Each time, we followed the same strategy: we wrote down the crossing prediction, isolated the conjectured cut term, and compared it explicitly with the result of a direct calculation using methods like Schwinger parameters or the embedding space formalism. To achieve the goal of this section, it remains to perform similar checks on the five-point pentagon topology. As we will detail shortly, we will undertake these checks using the method of differential equations. This method is quite general and should be suitable to rigorously test the crossing equation for higher-loop examples or for examples that depend on more kinematic scales. At the same time, this demonstrates how the differential equation approach can be used as a more economical method to perform checks for all bubbles and boxes
simultaneously
, as these are master integrals for the pentagon family.

5.4
Pentagon (via differential equations)

For the massless pentagon amplitude

\mathcal{M}^{\text{pent}}=\int~\frac{\mathrm{d}^{\text{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\text{D}/2}}~\frac{1}{\textsf{D}_{1}\textsf{D}_{2}\textsf{D}_{3}\textsf{D}_{4}\textsf{D}_{5}}\quad\text{with}\quad\textsf{D}_{n}=\Big(\ell+\sum_{i=2}^{n}p_{j-1}\Big)^{2}-i\varepsilon\,,

(156)

we will put crossing to the test in two ways: first, using the conventional method we just outlined (Sec.
5.4
) in the above summary, and then using a different approach (Sec.
5.5
), which will allow us to make a new kind of useful predictions. In the latter case, we will explore how crossing can be used to navigate between
time-ordered
amplitudes in disconnected physical channels or, equivalently, between initial conditions in different channels. The crossing equation is then tested by comparing the results with the explicit evaluation of the integral. In Sec.
5.5
, we will find perfect agreement between the two.

Multi-Regge limit and analytic boundary conditions

The multi-Regge kinematics is defined as a scattering process where the final-state particles are strongly ordered in rapidity and have comparable transverse momenta
Kuraev:1976ge
. For example, setting
s_{34}
to be the dominating variable in a five-point process, its
leading order
effect is equivalent to the parameterization

\displaystyle s_{34}=\frac{s}{x^{2}},\quad s_{23}=-\frac{s_{1}s_{2}}{s}z\bar{z},\quad s_{12}=\frac{s_{1}}{x},\quad s_{51}=\frac{s_{2}}{x},\quad s_{45}=-\frac{s_{1}s_{2}}{s}(1-z)(1-\bar{z})\,.

(162)

Here,
s,s_{1},s_{2},z
and
\bar{z}
are all fixed and of
\mathcal{O}(1)
in the limit
0<x\ll 1
. The limit is shown in Fig.
8
.

Caron-Huot:2020vlo
.
The simplicity of the one-loop pentagon alphabet is greatly influenced by the multi-Regge limit rationalizing the root
\sqrt{\Delta}
, since

\Delta=\frac{s_{1}^{2}s_{2}^{2}}{x^{4}}(z-\bar{z})^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(x^{-3}\right)\,,

(163)

in this kinematics. This leads to significant consequences, as the differential equation reveals that the alphabet can be factorized into three distinct and independent subalphabets
Chicherin:2018yne

\{x\}\,\cup\{s,s_{1},s_{2},s_{1}\pm s_{2}\}\cup\{z,\bar{z},1-z,1-\bar{z},z-\bar{z},1-z-\bar{z}\}\,.

(164)

For the example considered, the multi-Regge regime is particularly advantageous for establishing a basepoint (or initial condition). Among other things, it makes the transcendental weight structure of the master integrals manifest. A convenient point in this limit is the collinear point (equivalent to
s_{23}\to 0
)

X_{0}=\{s=1,\;s_{1}=1,\;s_{2}=1,\;z\to 0^{+},\;\bar{z}\to 0^{+}\}\,.

(165)

At
X_{0}
, we are at the boundary of the physical region (
\Delta=0
) and the integrals can be computed directly to give a simple vector of constants in terms of
\zeta
-values and powers of
\pi
. This can be observed by substituting
s=s_{1}=s_{2}=1
into the exact expression

\begin{split}\hskip-11.38092pt\frac{\vec{I}_{215\leftarrow 34}}{-r_{\Gamma}}&=\bigg(\mathrm{e}^{i\pi\epsilon}s_{2}^{-\epsilon},\mathrm{e}^{i\pi\epsilon}s^{-\epsilon},\mathrm{e}^{i\pi\epsilon}s_{1}^{-\epsilon},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R},-2\pi\epsilon\mathcal{R}(\cot\pi\epsilon{+}i),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log(-\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}){+}\Psi_{1}^{\epsilon}\big),\\
&\quad\qquad-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{2}}{s}{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log(-\tfrac{s_{2}}{s}){+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),0\bigg)^{\top}\,,\end{split}

(166)

with
r_{\Gamma}=\mathrm{e}^{\epsilon\gamma_{\text{E}}}C(\epsilon)
,
\mathcal{R}=\big(\frac{s}{s_{1}s_{2}}\big)^{\epsilon}
and

\displaystyle\qquad\Psi_{1}^{\epsilon}=2\pi\cot\pi\epsilon+\psi(\epsilon)+\gamma_{\text{E}}\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}=\tfrac{1}{\epsilon}+\pi\cot\pi\epsilon+\psi(\epsilon)+\gamma_{\text{E}}\,,

(167)

where
\psi(x)=\partial_{x}\log\Gamma(x)
is the digamma function. Note that (
166
) is valid within the
215\leftarrow 34
channel region carved by
\{s>0,s_{1}>0,s_{2}>0,z\to 0^{+},\bar{z}\to 0^{+}\}
. This expression was obtained by directly expanding in the multi-Regge-collinear limit the properly normalized bubble and box expressions in
Kozlov:2015kol
.

Checking crossing

From a computation similar to the one leading to (
166
), we find

\begin{split}\hskip-11.38092pt\frac{\vec{I}_{315\leftarrow 24}^{~{\dagger}}}{-r_{\Gamma}}&=\!\bigg(\!\mathrm{e}^{-i\pi\epsilon}s_{2}^{-\epsilon},(-s)^{-\epsilon},(-s_{1})^{-\epsilon},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R},-2\epsilon\pi\mathcal{R}(\cot\pi\epsilon{-}i),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}{-}i\pi{+}\Psi_{1}^{\epsilon}\big),\\
&-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}~\big(\log\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}~\big(\log(\tfrac{s_{2}}{-s}){+}i\pi{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}~\big(\log(\tfrac{s_{2}}{-s}){+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),0\bigg)^{\top},\end{split}

(168)

within the
315\leftarrow 24
channel
\{s<0,s_{1}<0,s_{2}>0,z\to 0^{+},\bar{z}\to 0^{+}\}
multi-Regge-collinear region.

Together, the standard amplitudes in (
166
) and (
168
) provide enough information to predict a cut using our crossing conjecture. Starting with (
168
) in the
315\leftarrow 24
channel, suppose we cross particles
2
and
3
. Under this crossing, both
s
and
s_{1}
rotate from negative to positive in the
upper
half-plane (because we start with the
conjugated
amplitude (
168
)), while all the other Mandelstam variables remain fixed. Substituting
s\to-|s|\mathrm{e}^{-i\phi}
and
s_{1}\to-|s_{1}|\mathrm{e}^{-i\phi}
into (
168
), we find (at
\phi=\pi
)

\displaystyle\hskip-11.38092pt{\left[\eqref{eq:bdryCTE2}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{\phantom{1}}\\
\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{1}\end{subarray}}}

\displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{e}^{-i\pi\epsilon}s_{2}^{-\epsilon},\mathrm{e}^{i\pi\epsilon}s^{-\epsilon},\mathrm{e}^{i\pi\epsilon}s_{1}^{-\epsilon},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R},-2\pi\epsilon\mathcal{R}(\cot\pi\epsilon{-}i),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}{-}i\pi{+}\Psi_{1}^{\epsilon}\big),\right.

\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt\left.-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{1}}{s}{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log\tfrac{s_{2}}{s}{+}2\pi i{+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),-2\epsilon\mathcal{R}\big(\log(-\tfrac{s_{2}}{s}){+}\Psi_{2}^{\epsilon}\big),0\right)^{\top}\,.

(169)

Verifying crossing in the multi-Regge-collinear regime
\{s>0,s_{1}>0,s_{2}>0,z\to 0^{+},\bar{z}\to 0^{+}\}
thus amounts to checking if

\left[\vec{I}_{315\leftarrow 24}^{~{\dagger}}\right]_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{\phantom{1}}\\
\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s_{1}\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}-\vec{I}_{215\leftarrow 34}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{15}}\vec{I}_{215\leftarrow 34}\,.

(170)

Note that the right-hand-side here is a non-trivial cut that cannot be deduced solely from the Cutkosky rules.

To check if (
170
) is correct, we compute the
s_{15}
-cut directly and expand the result in the multi-Regge-collinear region where (
166
) is defined. Using the embedding space formalism outlined earlier, we obtain (in generic kinematics):

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{15}}\vec{I}_{215\leftarrow 34}=2ir_{\Gamma}s_{51}^{-\epsilon}\sin(\pi\epsilon)\left(1,\vec{0}_{4},-\mathcal{F}\left(\tfrac{s_{34,51}}{s_{12}}\right),-\mathcal{F}\left(\tfrac{s_{23,51}}{s_{45}}\right),0,\mathcal{F}\left(\tfrac{s_{51,23}s_{51,34}}{s_{23}s_{34}}\right),0,\bullet\right)^{\top}

\displaystyle\text{with}\quad s_{ij,kl}\equiv s_{ij}-s_{kl}\ \text{and}\ \mathcal{F}(Z)\equiv 2~{}_{2}F_{1}\left(1,-\epsilon;1-\epsilon;1-Z\right)\,.

(171)

The dot “
\bullet
” indicates that the computation of the pentagon cut is omitted, since it is sufficient to know it vanishes at
\Delta=0
for the purpose of this calculation.

Upon comparing the multi-Regge-collinear expansion of (
5.4
) with (
170
), we observe a perfect match.

At this point, we would like to emphasize that there is no loss of generality in checking crossing in just the multi-Regge-collinear regime. Indeed, since both the master integrals and the cuts satisfy the
same
differential equation, checking crossing at a single point in the kinematic space is sufficient. Checking it elsewhere (for instance, away from
\Delta=0
where the pentagon contribution does
not
vanish) is equivalent to integrating the differential equation in App.
D
with the initial condition determined by the data where the crossing is already established.

5.5
Application: All time-ordered amplitudes from a single one

An interesting application of crossing symmetry involves asking if there are paths in the kinematic space that could serve as bridges between the

(174)

It is evident that these two limits are equivalent through an up-down reflection of the diagrams. In fact, one can verify through direct computations that the vectors of master integrals
\vec{I}
at
\theta=0
and
\theta=\pi/2
are permutations of each other (thus justifying the name!), precisely matching the reflection prediction.

On the other hand, the most complicated move is realized through the
crossing path
, which will be our main focus below. While most of the technical details associated with it are postponed to the next section and example, let us just say that, starting from the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}\ell}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}j}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}i}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}m}
amplitude, this move returns the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}\ell}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}m}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}i}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}j}
one.

Finally, even though the
permutation paths
are encountered as interim steps of the crossing path (as will be discussed below), they stand as legitimate paths in their own right: they are used to exchange either a pair of incoming or outgoing particles. Along such paths, the sign of individual invariant remains unchanged, while the overall rapidity ordering gets shuffled around.

:
All crossing relations between permutations of the one-mass box.
Looping arrows denote crossing moves that result in the same configuration up to a relabeling of the Mandelstam variables.

To see this, it is helpful to circle back to momenta. For a generic five-point process
k\ell m\leftarrow ij
, the multi-Regge kinematics is characterized by a fast propagation of the in states (
i
and
j
) along the
\mp
light-cone axes, and a strong ordering of the out-states (
k
,
\ell
, and
m
) based on the rapidity scale
0<x\ll 1
. In other words, while the outgoing momenta are organized as

p_{k}^{\mu}=\left(\frac{p_{k}^{+}}{x},\,xp_{k}^{-},\,p^{\perp}_{k}\right),\quad\ p_{\ell}^{\mu}=\left(p_{\ell}^{+},\,p_{\ell}^{-},\,p^{\perp}_{\ell}\right),\quad\ p_{m}^{\mu}=\left(xp_{m}^{+},\,\frac{p_{m}^{-}}{x},\,p^{\perp}_{m}\right)\,,

(175)

momentum conservation requires the incoming momenta to be

p_{i}^{\mu}=-\left(0,\frac{p_{m}^{-}}{x}+p_{\ell}^{-}+xp_{k}^{-},0^{\perp}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad p_{j}^{\mu}=-\left(\frac{p_{k}^{+}}{x}+p_{\ell}^{+}+xp_{m}^{+},0,0^{\perp}\right)\,,

(176)

where
p^{\perp}_{k}+p^{\perp}_{\ell}+p^{\perp}_{m}=0^{\perp}
in the transverse direction. The on-shell condition is
p^{\perp}\cdot p^{\perp}=p^{+}p^{-}
, and all “
\pm
” quantities are assumed to be non-zero. Plugging (
175
) and (
176
) into

s_{ab}=p_{a}^{+}p_{b}^{-}+p_{b}^{+}p_{a}^{-}-2p_{a}^{\perp}\cdot p_{b}^{\perp}\quad\text{for}\quad a,b\in\{i,j,k,\ell,m\}\,,

(177)

it is not hard to see the dramatic effect on the kinematics following the label permutation in e.g.,
(ii)
below: some of the original scales of order
1/x^{2}
become finite after the rotation (e.g.,
s_{ij}
), and vice versa (e.g.,
s_{im}
and
s_{kj}
). In other words, the original kinematic domain and the target kinematic domain are described by two
parametrically disconnected
multi-Regge limits.

Therefore, to move from one domain to the other, we first need to step
out
of the former and then step
into
the latter, through a finite rapidity region. At the very end of this subsection, we will illustrate this procedure through an explicit example.

Before moving on to the full master basis example, we find it instructive to pause and discuss how crossing relates amplitudes with different labels on a single four-propagator master integral. For instance, one may be interested in relating different channels of the same diagram. This is shown in Fig.
9
in the case
of the five-point one-mass box
\mathcal{M}^{\text{box}}=\mathcal{M}_{0a_{j}a_{k}a_{\ell}a_{m}}^{\text{pent}}
(whose functional form was given and studied earlier around (
137
)).

Of particular interest is the fact that the central diagram connects with all the others. Thus, as soon as the central diagram and all its cuts are known, one can deduce the amplitude in all the other channels. Since the central diagram only has one cut, it can be obtained from its imaginary part from the usual Cutkosky rules. Hence, it suffices to start with the conventional time-ordered diagram to deduce all the others by crossing.

Crossing path between time-ordered amplitudes

The purpose of this section is to provide the schematic instructions on how to obtain the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}\ell}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}m}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}i}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}j}
time-ordered amplitude from the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}\ell}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}j}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,1}i}{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}m}
one, by a composition of crossing moves and permuting labels. This procedure is a special case of (
71
) and generalizes to arbitrary multiplicity
Mizera:2021fap
. This section is followed by a concrete example that provides explicit equations to support what is discussed here.

Above, the color code mimics the one used in the previous sections: the red lines are the ones crossed between the two time-ordered amplitudes. In particular, we see that it is organized into three steps. To each of them, we associate a path along which we transport an initial condition such that:

At this stage, the distinction between “crossing” and “permuting” may not be clear. The key observation is that, while

67
)),
(ii)
leaves the sign of the invariant unchanged, but
significantly
alter the rapidity dependence of certain scales.

We now illustrate how to use the crossing path between time-ordered amplitudes through an explicit example.

and

\gamma_{A\to B}=\left\{s(\phi)=\mathrm{e}^{i\phi}\left|s\right|,s_{1}(\phi)=\mathrm{e}^{i\phi}\left|s_{1}\right|\;\left|\;0\leqslant\phi\leqslant\pi\right.\right\}\,.

Next,

\gamma_{C\to D}=\left\{s(\phi)=\mathrm{e}^{-i\phi}\left|s\right|,s_{1}(\phi)=\mathrm{e}^{-i\phi}\left|s_{1}\right|\;\left|\;0\leqslant\phi\leqslant\pi\right.\right\}\,,

parametrized from (

We note that the crossing steps

-1&0&\frac{1}{12}\pi^{2}&\frac{7}{3}\zeta_{3}&\frac{47}{1440}\pi^{4}&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}2}\\
-1&-i\pi&\frac{7}{12}\pi^{2}&\big(\frac{7}{3}\zeta_{3}+\frac{i}{4}\pi^{3}\big)&\big(\frac{7i}{3}\pi\zeta_{3}-\frac{73}{1440}\pi^{4}\big)&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}2}\\
2&2i\pi&-\frac{7}{6}\pi^{2}&-\big(\frac{14}{3}\zeta_{3}+\frac{i}{2}\pi^{3}\big)&\big(\frac{73}{720}\pi^{4}-\frac{14i}{3}\pi\zeta_{3}\big)&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}2}\\
2&2i\pi&-\frac{3}{2}\pi^{2}&-\big(\frac{20}{3}\zeta_{3}+\frac{i}{6}\pi^{3}\big)&-\big(\frac{43}{720}\pi^{4}+\frac{14i}{3}\pi\zeta_{3}\big)&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}1}\\
2&0&-\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}&-\frac{20}{3}\zeta_{3}&-\frac{43}{720}\pi^{4}&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}1}\\
2&0&-\frac{1}{6}\pi^{2}&-\frac{14}{3}\zeta_{3}&-\frac{47}{720}\pi^{4}&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}1}\\
0&0&0&\frac{1}{2}\pi\mathfrak{Li}_{2}-\frac{i}{54}\pi^{3}&\begin{subarray}{c}\frac{9}{65}\mathfrak{Li}_{2}^{2}+\frac{131i}{9}\pi^{2}\mathfrak{Li}_{2}+\frac{97}{520}\pi\mathfrak{Li}_{3}\\
-\frac{11i}{9}\mathfrak{Li}_{4}+\frac{7i}{9}\pi\zeta_{3}+\frac{23}{520}\pi^{4}\\
-\frac{69}{520}\pi^{2}\log^{2}3-\frac{13i}{3}\pi^{3}\log 3\end{subarray}&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}1}\\
\end{array}.\end{split}

(184)

The above result for the bubble and box integrals were cross-verified by directly evaluating the closed-form formulae in
Kozlov:2015kol
at endpoint
D
in the multi-Regge limit. The agreement between these quantities is yet another successful stress test for the crossing equation.

6
Analytic obstruction to crossing massive particles in gapless theories

Our conjecture for crossing described in Sec.
3.1
and
3.5
is based on two key ingredients:
analyticity of the Green’s function in off-shell kinematics, and the existence of an extension of this domain to scattering amplitudes on the mass shell.
In this section, we show that the second ingredient can, in principle, fail. We present a simple example where the time-ordered amplitude cannot be analytically continued to an inclusive observable without leaving the mass shell. This feature is closely tied to the existence of anomalous thresholds and is not unexpected from the axiomatic point of view. Indeed, it is known that beyond
4
-point scattering, it might no longer be possible to represent S-matrix elements in terms of a
single
analytic function
Bros:1972jh
. What happens in practice is that two thresholds (here, normal and anomalous) need to be approached from opposite directions in the complex plane, giving rise to an analytic obstruction or a gridlock, even at high energies. We will explain this phenomenon from several different points of view.

The key features of this example will be the presence of massive external
and
massless internal lines.
Physically, this creates the possibility that internal excitations travel faster than external ones,
even in the Regge limit where they are both nearly luminal.

(185)

The dashed and solid lines represent particles with mass
m_{1}
and
m_{2}
, while the wiggly line is a massless particle representing a graviton. This diagram depends only on three Mandelstam invariants, which we call
s
,
s_{1}
, and
s_{2}
, in addition to the two masses. For later convenience, at the start of the analytic continuation we will consider the complex-conjugated amplitude:

\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}=-\int\frac{\text{d}^{\mathrm{D}}\ell}{i\pi^{\mathrm{D}/2}}\frac{1}{[(\ell{-}p_{1})^{2}+m_{1}^{2}+i\varepsilon][(\ell{+}p_{2})^{2}+m_{2}^{2}+i\varepsilon][\ell^{2}+i\varepsilon]}\,,

(186)

which amounts to reversing the signs of
i
and the Feynman
i\varepsilon
(we have omitted coupling constants for simplicity). The prediction of the crossing equation is that exchanging particles
2\leftrightarrow 2^{\prime}
leads to

Here,
s=-p^{2}
rotates from negative to positive in the upper half-plane, with all the other invariants fixed. The reason why the rotation is clockwise is because we started with complex-conjugated amplitude.
In equations, we have

[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}\,\equiv\,\mathrm{Exp}_{2}\,,

(190)

where
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
denotes the contribution from the second diagram on the right-hand side of (
6.1
).
The quantity on the right-hand side is the in-in expectation value of an observable with momentum
2^{\prime}
,
\mathrm{Exp}_{2}
.

The goal of this section is to explain why this equation breaks down when particle
2
is massive and on shell with
s_{2}=m_{2}^{2}
. To illustrate this point, we will start with the off-shell configuration, say
s_{2}<m_{2}^{2}
, and show that the crossing path is cut off as we tune
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
. Physically, this phenomenon will have an explanation originating from the triangle anomalous threshold and that we cannot analytically continue around it when
s_{2}
is on-shell. We also take
s_{1}>m_{1}^{2}
in order to make the problem non-trivial:
if
s_{1}
were spacelike, the triangle could be viewed as part of a
2\to 2
scattering process for which crossing is already well established.

Our interest in studying this specific configuration comes from inquiring into limitations of crossing symmetry when crossing a massive particle in a gapless theory. This question becomes particularly important in applications to computing gravitational waveforms, in which potential-scattering diagrams of the form (
185
) appear. The intuition developed in this section will help us decide about the path of analytic continuation between time-ordered amplitudes and expectation values of gravitational radiation. In particular, we will be able to understand why the issues described here go away when crossing a graviton instead of a massive particle.

6.2
Analytic continuation in Schwinger parameters

While we could illustrate this idea with explicit expressions, they would not be entirely illuminating. For example, in
\mathrm{D}=4
, the result of
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}
is written in terms of dilogarithms with square roots depending on the scales
s,s_{1},s_{2},m_{1}
and
m_{2}
. Instead, we are going to manipulate
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}
entirely at the level of integrals to work out under which conditions (
190
) holds. It will also illustrate how the unitarity cuts that arise can be represented in their Schwinger-parametric form.

Denoting Schwinger parameters of the three propagators by
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}
and
\alpha_{3}
, corresponding to the internal edges of masses
m_{1}
,
m_{2}
and
0
, respectively, the parametric form of the integral reads

\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\text{d}\alpha_{1}\text{d}\alpha_{3}}{(\alpha_{1}+1+\alpha_{3})\left[A(\alpha_{1})+\alpha_{3}B(\alpha_{1})+i\varepsilon\right]}\,,

(191)

with

A\equiv(\alpha_{1}+1)(\alpha_{1}m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2})-\alpha_{1}s\quad\text{and}\quad B\equiv\alpha_{1}(m_{1}^{2}-s_{1})+m_{2}^{2}-s_{2}\,.

(192)

Recall that the
\alpha_{i}
’s are determined only up to an overall rescaling, and here we set
\alpha_{2}=1
, with the other two integrated from
0
to
\infty
.
The Feynman
i\varepsilon
prescription can be alternatively implemented by giving
s
a small
negative
imaginary part, i.e., by approaching the real axis from the lower half-plane.
However, the crossing equation instructs us to continue in the upper half-plane.

It turns out that the integral representation (
191
) gives a branch cut along the whole real
s
-axis. (Recall that branch points are properties of the function itself, but placements of branch cuts are specific to a given representation.) It is the so-called
external mass singularity
, see
Hannesdottir:2022bmo
. The way to understand why it arises is to think of assigning
\pm i\varepsilon
to
s_{1}
instead of including it as a separate factor, which is entirely equivalent. Since
s_{1}>m_{1}^{2}
is above the threshold, the two choices
s_{1}\pm i\varepsilon
clearly give different answers: they differ by a unitarity cut in the
s_{1}
-channel. But mathematically, this procedure is analogous to setting
s\pm i\varepsilon
for any real
s
.
This is why the above representation exhibits a discontinuity across the whole
s
-axis. This is not a problem by itself. We just need to analytically continue the representation through the branch cut at
s<0
to get access to the upper half-plane, instead of blindly inserting
s+i\varepsilon
.

As promised, we will perform this analytic continuation at the level of the integral. Since
s<0
and
m_{1},m_{2}>0
at the beginning of the continuation, we know that
A>0
across the entire integration domain. On the other hand,
B
can change sign depending on the value of
\alpha_{1}
. In particular, we have
B<0
for

\alpha_{1}>\alpha_{1*}=-\frac{s_{2}-m_{2}^{2}}{s_{1}-m_{1}^{2}}>0\,.

(193)

For any fixed
\alpha_{1}
satisfying this inequality, the discontinuity we are looking for is given by

\frac{1}{A+\alpha_{3}B+i\varepsilon}=\frac{1}{A+\alpha_{3}B-i\varepsilon}-2\pi i\,\delta(A+\alpha_{3}B)\,.

(194)

As such, we can rewrite the conjugated amplitude as

\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}-2\pi i\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\text{d}\alpha_{1}\text{d}\alpha_{3}}{(\alpha_{1}+1+\alpha_{3})}\,\delta\left[A(\alpha_{1})+\alpha_{3}B(\alpha_{1})\right]\,.

(195)

The first term on the right-hand side is simply the amplitude
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
without the complex conjugate, for any real
s
when approaching from the upper half-plane. The second one gives a new term, which allows us to localize
\alpha_{3}
around
\alpha_{3*}=-\tfrac{A}{B}>0
using the
\delta
-function with
\delta(A+\alpha_{3}B)=-\frac{1}{B}\delta(\alpha_{3}-\alpha_{3*})
.
This procedure is, of course, equivalent to deforming the
\alpha_{3}
-contour and picking up an extra residue. In the end, we find that

[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s}=\mathrm{Exp}_{2}+\Delta\,,

(196)

where we have factored out the expected answer (
190
)
and the “error”
\Delta
is the difference between the continued residue and a cut:

\Delta=\underbracket{2\pi i\int_{\alpha_{1*}}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha_{1}}{(\alpha_{1}+1)B(\alpha_{1})-A(\alpha_{1})}}_{C(s)}\,-\,\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}\,.

(197)

The integral does not have any singularities in the upper half-plane of
s
when the remaining kinematics is real. This is guaranteed by the fact that
\mathrm{Im}\,A<0
for any
\mathrm{Im}\,s>0
and hence its denominator always stays non-zero.
The remaining challenge is to show that,
after taking its limit to the real
axis at large positive
s
, it agrees precisely with the cut term, so that

\Delta\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}0\,.

(198)

In the above,
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
is defined for real positive
s
by the on-shell cut integral in (
6.1
); we will also discuss below its continuation into the upper half-plane of
s
.

At this stage, it is instructive to analyze the singularities that can potentially arise from the integrals
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
and
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
when approached from the upper half-plane. There are three relevant singularities: the
s
-channel normal threshold, the leading second-type singularity, and the triangle anomalous thresholds. The first one arises when

(\alpha_{1}:\alpha_{2}:\alpha_{3})=\left(\pm\tfrac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}:1:0\right)\quad\text{and}\quad s=(m_{1}\pm m_{2})^{2}\,.

(199)

The second one happens for

(\alpha_{1}:\alpha_{2}:\alpha_{3})=\left(\pm\tfrac{\sqrt{s_{2}}}{\sqrt{s_{1}}}:1:-1\mp\tfrac{\sqrt{s_{2}}}{\sqrt{s_{1}}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad s=(\sqrt{s_{1}}\pm\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}\,.

(200)

In both cases, only the first choice of signs gives a singularity of
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
on the relevant sheet.
Finally, the triangle anomalous threshold occurs for

(\alpha_{1}:\alpha_{2}:\alpha_{3})=(\alpha_{1*}:1:\alpha_{3*}(\alpha_{1*}))\quad\text{and}\quad s=s_{*}\equiv m_{1}^{2}\left(1-\frac{s_{2}-m_{2}^{2}}{s_{1}-m_{1}^{2}}\right)+(1\leftrightarrow 2)\,.

(201)

Here, crucially,
\alpha_{3*}(\alpha_{1*})=-\lim_{\alpha_{1}\to\alpha_{1\ast}}\tfrac{A(\alpha_{1})}{B(\alpha_{1})}
is evaluated at the specific value
\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{1*}
(defined in (
193
)) and does
not
have to be positive. Explicitly, it reads

\alpha_{3*}(\alpha_{1*})=\frac{m_{2}^{2}}{s_{2}-m_{2}^{2}}-m_{1}^{2}\frac{s_{2}-m_{2}^{2}}{(s_{1}-m_{1}^{2})^{2}}\,.

(202)

Since we are interested in the kinematics with
s_{1}>m_{1}^{2}
, as
s_{2}<m_{2}^{2}
approaches the threshold
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
, the corresponding
\alpha_{3*}\to-\infty
. In particular, the fact that
\alpha_{3*}
is negative means that the singularity does not occur on the sheet of
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
in the upper half-plane we are exploring now. This argument does not apply to the correction term
C
in (
197
) nor to
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
, because
\alpha
-positivity only holds for singularities of time-ordered amplitudes on the first sheet.
We will see that, indeed, the anomalous threshold
does
appear for these.

The anomalous threshold at
s=s_{\ast}
manifests itself as an endpoint singularity of
C
at
\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{1*}
, where the integrand denominator for
C
becomes

(\alpha_{1*}+1)B(\alpha_{1*})-A(\alpha_{1*})=\alpha_{1*}(s-s_{\ast})\,,

(203)

which shows that
C
develops a logarithmic singularity at
s=s_{\ast}
. The sign of
\alpha_{3*}
is irrelevant since it is no longer an integration variable. This can be verified explicitly by evaluating its integral representation in (
197
). We indeed find

\displaystyle C(s)

\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{-\lambda}}\left(\log\frac{i\sqrt{-\lambda}+(s-s_{1}-s_{2}-2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast})}{i\sqrt{-\lambda}-(s-s_{1}-s_{2}-2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast})}-i\pi\right),

(204)

where
\lambda\equiv s^{2}+s_{1}^{2}+s_{2}^{2}-2ss_{1}-2ss_{2}-2s_{1}s_{2}\,
is the
Källén/triangle function
. One of its zeros is at
s=(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}
, which is the square-root second-type singularity. This threshold is also the lower limit of the physical region,
s>(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}
for the
1^{\prime}23\leftarrow 12^{\prime}
kinematics.
The branches of the square roots were carefully chosen so that the above formula is valid in the upper half-plane of
s
.

The analyticity of
{\rm Exp}_{2}
in the
s
-plane is summarized in Fig.
11
, where we added a small positive imaginary part to
s_{2}
to more clearly illustrate the sheet structure.

s
\times
\times
(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}
s_{\tiny*}
(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}

Figure 11
:

Left:

The analytic structure of
\mathrm{Exp}_{2}

in the complex
s
-plane for
m_{1}=m_{2}=1
,
s_{1}=5
, and
s_{2}=0.9+0.01i
. We observe a branch cut starting at the normal threshold at
s=(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}=4
up to infinity, another extending to the triangle anomalous threshold at
s=s_{\ast}\approx 41.6+4i
from the leading second-type singularity at
s=(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}\approx 10.1+0.03i
. The physical region in the
s
channel starts at the second-type singularity
s=(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}
, and extends to
s\to\infty
.
In the on-shell limit,
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
, the anomalous threshold behaves as
s_{\ast}\to-m_{2}^{2}\frac{s_{1}-m_{1}^{2}}{s_{2}-m_{2}^{2}}
and hence moves to infinity, thus cutting off
the inclusive observable from the analytic continuation of
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}
. The branch cut along the real axis is the external mass singularity.

Right:
A schematic figure of the analytic structure of
\mathrm{Exp}_{2}
in the complex
s
-plane. The branch cuts are marked in yellow. We observe two possible paths of analytic continuation in the upper half-plane, marked in red and blue, which differ by how the anomalous threshold at
s^{\ast}
is traversed. The red dashed path is the one that would be reached without deforming
s^{\ast}
to be complex, and does not correspond to
\text{Exp}_{2}
. The solid blue path, on the other hand, is the one that reaches the real axis where the inclusive observable
\text{Exp}_{2}
is defined.

6.3
Comparison with unitarity cuts

Let us now compare
C
with the cut
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
predicted by (
190
) and check if (
198
) is satisfied. The latter is given by

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}\equiv-(2\pi i)^{2}\int\frac{\text{d}^{4}\ell}{i\pi^{2}}\frac{\delta^{+}(\ell^{2})\,\delta^{-}[(\ell{-}p_{1})^{2}+m_{1}^{2}]}{(\ell{+}p_{2})^{2}+m_{2}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,.

(205)

Our goal is to massage this expression into a form similar to
C
. In the
s_{1}
rest frame, the momentum vectors can be written as

\displaystyle p_{1}

\displaystyle=\big(\sqrt{s_{1}},\,0,\,0,\,0\big)\,,

(206a)

\displaystyle p_{2}

\displaystyle=\big(\tfrac{s{-}s_{1}{-}s_{2}}{2\sqrt{s_{1}}},\,0,\,0,\,\tfrac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\sqrt{s_{1}}}\big)\,,

(206b)

\displaystyle p

\displaystyle=\big(\tfrac{{-}s{-}s_{1}{+}s_{2}}{2\sqrt{s_{1}}},\,0,\,0,\,{-}\tfrac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2\sqrt{s_{1}}}\big)\,,

(206c)

\displaystyle\ell

\displaystyle=\big(\ell^{0},\,|\vec{\ell}|\cos\varphi\sin\theta,\,|\vec{\ell}|\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\,|\vec{\ell}|\cos\theta\big)\,.

(206d)

In this frame, the two
\delta
-functions impose

-(\ell^{0})^{2}+|\vec{\ell}|^{2}=0\quad\text{and}\quad-(\ell^{0}-\sqrt{s_{1}})^{2}+|\vec{\ell}|^{2}+m_{1}^{2}=0\,.

(207)

Together, they fix
\ell^{0}_{*}=|\vec{\ell}|_{*}=\frac{s_{1}-m_{1}^{2}}{2\sqrt{s_{1}}}
. Imposing positivity of the energies flowing through the cut (
\ell^{0}>0
and
\ell^{0}-p_{1}^{0}<0
) amounts to
s_{1}>m_{1}^{2}
, meaning we are, as needed, above the
s_{1}
-threshold. On the support of these constraints, the leftover propagator in (
205
) is

(\ell{+}p_{2})^{2}+m_{2}^{2}=-s_{2}-2\ell^{0}_{*}(p_{2}^{0}-p_{2}^{3}\cos\theta)+m_{2}^{2}\,,

(208)

where the components
p_{2}^{0}
and
p_{2}^{3}
are given in (
206b
). Hence, after going to spherical coordinates
and localizing along
\ell^{0}=\ell^{0}_{*}
and
|\vec{\ell}|=|\vec{\ell}|_{*}
(with a Jacobian of
\tfrac{1}{4\sqrt{s_{1}}\ell^{0}_{*}}
coming from the
\delta
-functions) we arrive at

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}

\displaystyle=-\frac{2\pi i\ell^{0}_{*}}{\sqrt{s_{1}}}\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\text{d}\cos\theta}{-s_{2}-2\ell^{0}_{*}\big(p_{2}^{0}-p_{2}^{3}\cos\theta\big)+m_{2}^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,.

(209)

The only kinematic assumption here is that
s_{1}>m_{1}^{2}
, ensuring that the cut has support. This representation can be used for any real
p_{2}^{\mu}
and thus real
s
.
Its continuation to complex
s
will turn out to be different depending on whether
s
is above or below the triangle anomalous threshold at
s=s_{\ast}
.

Let us first check whether
\Delta=0
in real
s
-channel kinematics (i.e., for
s>(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}
), by massaging the cut contribution (
209
) into a form that resembles the
\alpha_{1}
integral from (
197
). To this end, we start by combining the regions with
\pm\cos\theta
and
change variable to
x=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}
to get

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}=4\pi i\int_{1}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}x\frac{-s+s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast}}{\lambda-x^{2}(-s+s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast})^{2}-i\varepsilon}\,,

(210)

where we have assumed that
s>s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast}
for the change of variables, which always holds when
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
.
Next, we shift and rescale
x
by defining
\alpha_{1}=\tfrac{-s+s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast}}{2s_{1}}x+\frac{s-s_{1}-s_{2}}{2s_{1}}
and end up with

\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}=2\pi i\int^{-\infty}_{\alpha_{1*}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha_{1}}{(\alpha_{1}+1)B(\alpha_{1})-A(\alpha_{1})-i\varepsilon}\,.

(211)

Here, we have
-\infty
and not
+\infty
in the integration domain because
s
is taken to be large enough such that
s>s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{1}\alpha_{1\ast}
. Moreover, the coefficient of
i\varepsilon
after these changes of variables is

(s_{1}+s_{2}-s+2s_{1}\alpha_{1})^{2}
, which we drop because it is always positive in physical kinematics.

Figure 12
:

Left:
The integration contour in
\cos\theta
for
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
. The integral has a real part when
s>s_{\ast}
(a), but is purely imaginary when
s<s_{\ast}
(c).

Right:
The two contributions to the integration contour for
\Delta
, from
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
(blue) and
C(s)
(red). The points
\alpha_{-}
and
\alpha_{+}
correspond to the two roots of the denominator that appear in the integrand of
\Delta
. When
s>s_{\ast}
(b), the red and blue contours can be deformed into each other, resulting in
\Delta=0
. When
s<s_{\ast}
(d), the difference between the red and blue contours can be deformed into one that encircles the root
\alpha_{-}
counter-clockwise.

Comparing (
197
) and (
211
) and dropping the
i\varepsilon
’s, we see that the
integrands
for
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
and
C(s)
are the same. Their integration contours are different, however, so to find the contribution to
\Delta
, we must first analyze which way the contour traverses around the singularities of the integrand. The singularities are at the two roots of the denominators:

\alpha_{\pm}=\frac{s-s_{1}-s_{2}\pm\sqrt{\lambda}}{2s_{1}}\,.

(212)

One can see from this expression that in the physical region for
\lambda>0
we have

\alpha_{1\ast}<\alpha_{\pm}\quad\text{for }s<s_{\ast}\quad\text{or}\quad\alpha_{-}<\alpha_{1\ast}<\alpha_{+}\quad\text{for }s>s_{\ast}\,.

(213)

The contour for
C(s)
runs from
\alpha_{1\ast}
to
\infty
, and approaches the roots with
s\to s+i\varepsilon
, which translates into the integration contour for
C(s)
being deformed into the upper half-plane around
\alpha_{-}
and into the lower half-plane around
\alpha_{+}
, as shown in Fig.
12
. The contour for
-\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
runs from
-\infty
to
\alpha_{1\ast}
, and when the root
\alpha_{-}
is on the contour for
s>s_{\ast}
, it must be approached by deforming the contour into the lower half-plane, as dictated by the
i\varepsilon
in (
211
). This is possible since the integrand in (
211
) has no residue at infinity.

We can now read the integration contour for
\Delta
from Fig
12
, as the sum of the contours for
C(s)
and
-\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
in the
\alpha
plane. On one hand, when
s>s_{\ast}
(see Fig
12
(b)), the contributions from
C(s)
and
-\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
add up to give a contour that can be deformed to zero, and hence
\Delta=0
when
s>s_{\ast}
. On the other hand, when
s<s_{\ast}
(see Fig
12
(d)), the two contours can be deformed around a small clockwise circle around
\alpha_{-}
(from (
212
)) in the
\alpha_{1}
-plane:

\Delta|_{s<s_{\ast}}=2\pi i\ointclockwise_{\alpha_{-}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha_{1}}{(\alpha_{1}+1)B(\alpha_{1})-A(\alpha_{1})}=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\,,

(214)

where we have evaluated the integral using the residue theorem, noting the overall minus sign because of the orientation.
To summarize,

\Delta=\begin{cases}0&\qquad\text{if }s>s_{\ast}\,,\\
\frac{4\pi^{2}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}&\qquad\text{if }(\sqrt{s_{1}}+\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}<s<s_{\ast}\,.\end{cases}

(215)

Finally, we can ask whether it is possible to analytically continue
C(s)
such that it agrees with
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
.
Inspection of the lower-right panel of Fig.
12
indicates that we need to continue in such a way that the root
\alpha_{-}
goes clockwise around
\alpha_{1\ast}
. Note that the collision
\alpha_{-}=\alpha_{1\ast}
occurs precisely at the anomalous threshold
s=s_{\ast}
.
In the
s
-plane, this can thus be achieved by taking
s
clockwise below
s_{\ast}
.
In other words, starting from large real
s>s_{\ast}
, we lower
s
passing at
s=s_{\ast}-i\varepsilon

below
the threshold, as indicated by the arrows
in Fig.
11
.

This construction is not possible in the on-shell limit when
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
, since the branch point at
s_{\ast}
moves to infinity:
a crossing path exists only off-shell.

The fact that the anomalous threshold must be avoided with
s-i\varepsilon
can also be seen directly from the endpoint singularities in (
209
). Since
\ell_{\ast}^{0}>0
, the contribution near the upper endpoint at
\cos\theta=1
is analytic for
{\rm Im}\,p_{2}^{+}>0
, while that from the lower endpoint
\cos\theta=-1
is analytic for
{\rm Im}\,p_{2}^{-}>0
. Since
p_{2}^{+}\propto s
while
p_{2}^{-}\propto\frac{1}{s}
, these singularities lie on opposite sides of the real
s
axis
(this is the “gridlock” mentioned at the top of this section).
The
s=s_{\ast}
branch point is caused by the lower endpoint.

To conclude this subsection, we briefly consider the consequences of analytically continuing
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}
from (
186
) in the loop-momentum space representation of
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
instead of in Schwinger-parameter space. Rather than computing the discontinuity across the branch cut in
s
for
s<0
as the term
C(s)
from (
197
), we could instead, by unitarity, evaluate
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
from (
209
). For
s<0
, we can, therefore, write

\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}\,.

(216)

Note that although this expression looks like the crossing equation, we have not done any analytic continuation in
s
, so we cannot conclude anything about crossing yet. To do so, we have to analytically continue
both
the left-hand side and right-hand side in the upper half-plane of
s
, and check whether

\left[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}^{\dagger}\right]_{\raisebox{0.0pt}{\scalebox{1}[1]{$\curvearrowright$}}s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}+\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}\,,

(217)

where the right-hand side should now be evaluated at
s>0
.

We recall that
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
is analytic in the upper half-plane of
s
, so
to answer the question of whether the crossing equation (
217
) holds, it is sufficient to ask whether
\mathrm{Cut}_{s_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{tri}}
from (
209
) evaluates to the same function for
s>0
and
s<0
. Let us take this opportunity to stress the important point that even though we write the same expression (
209
), for both
s<0
and
s>0
, it does not immediately follow that it evaluates to the same analytic function in both kinematic channels. In fact, as we found previously, the function for
s>0
is the same as the one for
s<0
if and only if
s>s_{\ast}
. We summarize the analytic properties of (
209
) in Fig.
13
, both in the
s
-plane and the
\cos\theta
-plane. We see from the figure that (
209
) is the same analytic function for
s>0
as for
s<0
only if
s>s^{\ast}
(Fig.
13
bottom left). As we found previously using the Schwinger-parametric form of
C(s)
, we can access the relevant sheet of
\mathrm{Exp}_{2}
by adding a small imaginary part to
s_{2}
(Fig.
13
bottom right). However, when
s_{2}
is on shell (Fig.
13
bottom middle), it is not possible to reach the sheet of
\mathrm{Exp}_{2}
starting from
\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}
.

1
\cos\theta

:

) is analytic in the upper half-plane of

to

. As a result, (

. In the plot we show this connection by adding a small positive imaginary component

) is identical to that of

6.4
Spacetime interpretation

The presence of the triangle anomalous threshold for the
{\rm Exp}_{2}
observable could have been anticipated by thinking about the position-space support of the inclusive amplitude.
In this subsection, we show this by considering the associated trajectories of particles using a time-folded version of the Coleman–Norton interpretation of anomalous thresholds for exclusive scattering amplitudes
Coleman:1965xm
. This will also allow us to understand why the anomalous threshold branch cut must be approached with an opposing kinematic
s\pm i\varepsilon
prescription compared to the normal-threshold cut, causing a clash in the on-shell limit.

Recall that anomalous thresholds correspond to kinematic configurations where all the on-shell internal momenta
q_{i}^{\mu}
of the diagram follow classical trajectories of particles interacting at the vertices located at
x_{j}^{\mu}
. The spacetime displacement between two vertices
(x_{j},x_{k})
connected by the momentum
q_{i}
is
x_{k}-x_{j}=\alpha_{i_{\ast}}q_{i_{\ast}}
, where
\alpha_{i_{\ast}}
and
q_{i_{\ast}}
are solutions of Landau equations, see, e.g.,
Hannesdottir:2022bmo
. Time-ordered amplitudes additionally require
\alpha_{i}\geqslant 0
for all
i
, but cuts do not have the same restriction. Since we found in (
202
) that
\alpha_{3\ast}<0
when
s_{2}\to m_{2}^{2}
, the triangle threshold is accessible only through the cut contribution in (
190
). Let us adopt the following labeling of vertices for the cut diagram:
